name: Brali Protocol Feed
description: Practical protocols that currently meet the Brali public quality and indexing bar, with Brali ontology classification.
license: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0; Brali names and logos are not licensed for reuse.
selection_rule: Only entries with evidence status reviewed or practical are included.
identity_rule: protocol_id identifies the underlying protocol. Future language versions should keep the same protocol_id and change the language field.
ontology_rule: Use ontology.domains/topics/methods/lenses for new integrations. life_area and growth_zone remain compatibility fields. topic-pending means the legacy collection identifies a Method or Lens but the specific Topic still requires editorial classification.
source_rule: External source URLs are exposed only for reviewed entries. A recorded but unreviewed source is not presented as supporting evidence in this feed.

entries.title: Action and Mood Observation Note
entries.description: Use a short note to compare an activity with what you noticed before and after it. Treat the note as observation, not proof that an activity caused a mood change.
entries.action: Write the situation, the activity you chose, how you felt before, and how you felt afterward. Add one alternative explanation so the note does not turn correlation into certainty.
entries.check_in: What did you observe, and what would be worth trying or discussing next without assuming the activity caused the change?

entries.title: Active Recall: Close the Notes and Make Memory Work
entries.description: Before rereading, hide the source and try to produce the answer from memory. Then check it, fix the misses, and practice application separately if the real goal is solving, speaking, writing, or doing. Familiarity feels nice; retrieval tells you what is actually available without the page in front of you.
entries.action: Choose a small set of material you want to retain. Hide the source and answer a question, explain the idea, or write what you remember. Check immediately enough to catch errors and repair them. Then, if success means solving, writing, speaking, calculating, or performing, practice that outcome too. Memory practice is useful; it is not a teleportation device to skill.
entries.check_in: What could I retrieve without looking? What was missing or wrong? If the real goal is application, could I actually use the knowledge in a relevant task?

entries.title: Adjust for Regressive Bias
entries.description: When recalling or estimating: - Use actual data: Base your judgment on numbers or facts rather than instinct. - Check extremes: Ask if you’re underestimating highs or overestimating lows. - Keep track: Maintain a log to compare memories with reality over time. Example: Track your work hours to see if your memory matches the actual effort.
entries.action: When recalling or estimating: - Use actual data: Base your judgment on numbers or facts rather than instinct. - Check extremes: Ask if you’re underestimating highs or overestimating lows. - Keep track: Maintain a log to compare memories with reality over time. Example: Track your work hours to see if your memory matches the actual effort.
entries.check_in: Check in when you rely on data instead of assumptions to adjust your memories.

entries.title: AI-Assisted Premortem
entries.description: Use an AI model as a brainstorming partner for possible failure modes, then verify important risks against the real plan before choosing mitigations.
entries.action: Describe the plan without sensitive information, ask an AI for plausible ways it could fail, group the suggestions, verify the important ones yourself, and choose mitigations only for risks that survive the check.
entries.check_in: Which risks were genuinely relevant after verification, and which model suggestions were generic, impossible, or based on missing context?

entries.title: Alternate Focused Work With Real Breaks
entries.description: Use a protected focus block followed by a real break, then adjust the length to your task, energy, and schedule instead of treating 90/30 as a biological rule.
entries.action: Choose one important task, protect a focus block from avoidable interruptions, then step away for a real break. Adjust both periods to your workload and energy rather than forcing a fixed 90/30 schedule.
entries.check_in: Was the focus block long enough to make progress, did the break actually feel like a break, and what duration would fit the next cycle better?

entries.title: Anchor Your Timeline
entries.description: To fix time distortions: - Use anchors: Connect events to specific dates or milestones. - Journal regularly: Write down events as they happen to track their timing. - Review your calendar: Check past schedules to confirm when things actually happened. Example: If you’re unsure when you last met a client, refer to your notes or calendar to avoid assuming it was more recent or distant.
entries.action: To fix time distortions: - Use anchors: Connect events to specific dates or milestones. - Journal regularly: Write down events as they happen to track their timing. - Review your calendar: Check past schedules to confirm when things actually happened. Example: If you’re unsure when you last met a client, refer to your notes or calendar to avoid assuming it was more recent or distant.
entries.check_in: Check in when you use tools to correct your perception of time.

entries.title: Ask a Few Questions Before You Start Learning
entries.description: Before reading, watching, or studying new material, try a few questions about the specific information you want to learn. Attempt an answer, then study and check it. Evidence supports better learning for the prequestioned information, not a general boost to everything else.
entries.action: Choose a small set of questions that point to information you genuinely want to learn. Before opening the explanation, reading the chapter, or watching the lesson, make a brief attempt at each answer even if you are unsure. Then study normally, paying attention when the material resolves those questions. Afterward, check the answers against the source. Use this to target important information, not as a claim that every unasked detail will also be learned better.
entries.check_in: After studying, can I answer the questions accurately without looking, and did the questions point me toward information that actually mattered?

entries.title: Ask AI for Failure Cases Before You Ship
entries.description: Give AI a feature, process, calculation, message, or workflow and ask for edge cases and failure modes. Treat the output as a candidate list, deduplicate it, verify relevance, and convert the useful cases into executable tests or checklist items.
entries.action: Describe the intended behavior, constraints, known happy path, and expensive failures. Ask for boundary cases, invalid inputs, state transitions, concurrency or timing issues where relevant, and user misunderstandings. Remove duplicates, verify each candidate against the real system, and write tests for the cases worth keeping.
entries.check_in: Did AI expose a failure I had not covered, and did I turn that idea into a check rather than merely admire the list?

entries.title: Ask for Feedback on One Specific Decision
entries.description: Give the reviewer context, ask one focused question, make the reply easy and decide what you will accept, test, discuss, defer or ignore.
entries.action: State the intended outcome and the current decision. Ask one focused question such as what is unclear, what assumption looks wrong or what should change first. Choose a reviewer who can judge that question, then record what you will accept, test, discuss, defer or ignore.
entries.check_in: What did I ask, what did the reviewer actually say, and what decision or test changed because of it?

entries.title: Ask Why Until a Goal Becomes Clearer
entries.description: Use repeated why questions to examine what is behind a goal, then turn the useful insight into a next step. Five questions are a prompt, not a requirement or a guarantee of finding one root cause.
entries.action: Write one goal or problem, ask why it matters, and continue asking why while each answer adds something useful. Stop when the answers become repetitive, speculative, or split into different causes. Then choose one next step or one assumption to check.
entries.check_in: Did the questions reveal a useful reason, assumption, or constraint, and what will I do or verify next?

entries.title: Attempt First, Use AI for Feedback, Retest Without It
entries.description: For learning tasks, make a genuine attempt before asking AI to explain, critique, or extend your work, then reproduce the target skill without assistance. Recent evidence on generative AI in education is mixed enough that the workflow should preserve learner activity rather than assume the chatbot itself improves learning.
entries.action: Name the skill you are actually trying to acquire. Attempt a problem, explanation, translation, derivation, or answer unaided. Ask AI to identify gaps, give a contrasting example, or explain one sticking point. Check the feedback against trusted material when accuracy matters, then perform a fresh attempt without AI.
entries.check_in: Can I now perform or explain the target skill without leaning on the AI output?

entries.title: Audit a Default Before Letting It Decide for You
entries.description: For a setting, subscription, workflow, or template with meaningful consequences, identify the current default, compare the relevant alternatives, and make a deliberate keep-or-change decision with an easy rollback when possible.
entries.action: Pick one consequential default, identify what is currently selected, state what you need from the setting or service, compare only the realistic alternatives, note switching costs and important constraints, make a keep-or-change decision, and record how to reverse it when reversal matters.
entries.check_in: What default did I inspect, what requirement mattered most, why did I keep or change it, and can I reverse the decision if the new choice is worse?

entries.title: Audit Workspace Friction Before Buying More Gear
entries.description: Inspect where a workspace makes the actual task harder to see, reach, switch, connect, or reset; change one layout variable; and keep the change only when it removes friction without creating a new problem.
entries.action: Choose one frequent task, walk through it slowly, note every unnecessary reach, obstruction, visibility issue, cable move, device swap, or reset, rank the friction points, change one reversible layout variable, use the task again, and keep or undo the change based on what became easier or harder.
entries.check_in: Which step in the task had avoidable friction, what single workspace change did I make, and did it remove that friction without moving the problem somewhere else?

entries.title: Automate a Routine Report with Validation and Fallback
entries.description: Automate a stable reporting workflow only after defining source ownership, transformations, validation rules, freshness, failure handling, and a manual fallback.
entries.action: Map the report consumer, source data, transformations and delivery step. Define validation rules for schema, completeness, freshness and key totals. Build a small automated path with logging and a visible failure state, keep a manual fallback, and stop publication when validation fails.
entries.check_in: Did the automated report use the expected source, pass validation, arrive on time, and fail visibly when an assumption broke?

entries.title: Automatic Savings Rule
entries.description: If essential obligations are covered, automate a modest transfer to savings and review whether the amount remains comfortable. This is general educational guidance, not individualized financial advice.
entries.action: Review upcoming essential expenses, choose a small transfer amount you can change or cancel, schedule it after income arrives, and check that it does not create a shortfall.
entries.check_in: Did the automation make saving easier without making bills, debt payments, or necessary spending harder to cover?

entries.title: Avoid Boundary Extension Errors
entries.description: When recalling visuals: - Focus on details: Try to actively recall both the foreground and the background. - Verify: Revisit the original image or scene to compare your memory. - Practice recall: Test yourself on visual memories to sharpen your accuracy. Example: After seeing a photo, draw it from memory and then compare it to the original.
entries.action: When recalling visuals: - Focus on details: Try to actively recall both the foreground and the background. - Verify: Revisit the original image or scene to compare your memory. - Practice recall: Test yourself on visual memories to sharpen your accuracy. Example: After seeing a photo, draw it from memory and then compare it to the original.
entries.check_in: Check in when you actively verify your visual memory of an image or scene.

entries.title: Avoid Overestimating the Present: - Zoom Out: Ask, “will This Matter in a Year
entries.description: To avoid overestimating the present: - Zoom out: Ask, “Will this matter in a year? Five years?” - Review the past: Compare this moment to similar past events for perspective. - Plan ahead: Focus on long-term goals, not just immediate importance. Example: Instead of stressing over a minor setback, think about how it fits into your bigger picture.

Five years?” - Review the past: Compare this moment to similar past events for perspective. - Plan ahead: Focus on long-term goals, not just immediate importance. Example: Instead of stressing over a minor setback, think about how it fits into your bigger picture.
entries.check_in: Check in when you step back and see the broader context.

entries.title: Balance Leveling and Sharpening
entries.description: To keep memories accurate: - Write details down: Capture events as soon as possible to avoid losing information. - Check for gaps: Ask yourself what might be missing in your memory. - Avoid exaggeration: Be mindful of which details you emphasize when retelling stories. Example: After a meeting, jot down key points immediately before memories get distorted.

Example: After a meeting, jot down key points immediately before memories get distorted.
entries.check_in: Check in when you recall an event and actively balance details to avoid distortion.

entries.title: Balance Safety and Risk
entries.description: When safety increases: - Assess risks: Ask, "Am I compensating for safety by taking unnecessary risks?" - Set boundaries: Stick to cautious habits even in safer environments. - Focus on long-term impact: Remember that short-term safety doesn’t eliminate long-term consequences. Example: Driving a car with advanced safety features? Avoid speeding just because you feel more protected.

Example: Driving a car with advanced safety features? Avoid speeding just because you feel more protected.
entries.check_in: Check in when you avoid risky behaviors that counteract increased safety.

entries.title: Balance the Fading Affect Bias
entries.description: To stay balanced: - Acknowledge both sides: Write about unpleasant memories alongside the positive ones. - Reflect intentionally: Spend time thinking about what you learned from difficult moments. - Focus on growth: Use past challenges as a reminder of your resilience. Example: When recalling a failed project, consider the lessons learned rather than just forgetting the negatives.

Example: When recalling a failed project, consider the lessons learned rather than just forgetting the negatives.
entries.check_in: Check in when you balance fading negative emotions with the lessons they taught you.

entries.title: Balance the Negativity Bias
entries.description: To manage negative recall: - List positives: After a bad experience, write down at least 3 positive things that happened that day. - Reframe events: Find the silver lining in unpleasant memories. - Focus on solutions: Instead of dwelling on what went wrong, brainstorm ways to improve next time. Example: If a meeting didn’t go well, note what you learned and how you can prepare better next time.

Example: If a meeting didn’t go well, note what you learned and how you can prepare better next time.
entries.check_in: Check in when you counteract negativity by focusing on the positive.

entries.title: Batch Non-Urgent Notifications Instead of Receiving Them All Day
entries.description: Group non-urgent smartphone notifications into a few predictable delivery windows while keeping genuinely urgent channels available. The useful idea is predictable batching, not a magic number of batches.
entries.action: Choose the apps whose alerts are useful but rarely urgent. Use your phone's notification summary, scheduled focus mode, or another reversible setting to deliver those alerts in predictable windows. Keep calls, selected contacts, security alerts, calendars, or other genuinely time-sensitive channels outside the batch. Start with a schedule that fits your day rather than copying the study's three-times-a-day condition as a universal rule.
entries.check_in: Did I feel interrupted less often without creating missed urgent information, compulsive manual checking, or anxiety about what I could not see?

entries.title: Batch Routine Messages Around Real Response Obligations
entries.description: Set predictable windows for non-urgent messages, keep an explicit path for work that genuinely cannot wait, and adjust the schedule when it conflicts with actual response duties.
entries.action: List the communication channels you monitor, separate channels that require rapid coverage from routine messages, place routine processing into predictable windows, define an exception path for genuinely time-sensitive items, turn longer requests into tasks, and review whether your response obligations are still being met.
entries.check_in: Which messages waited until the planned window, which exception was genuinely time-sensitive, and did the schedule still meet the response expectations of my role?
keywords: Cut the Noise with Communication Blocks

entries.title: Batch Similar Tasks When Switching Is the Problem
entries.description: Group comparable low-risk tasks when repeated setup is slowing the work, then compare the batch with your normal flow and stop batching when responsiveness suffers.
entries.action: Pick one recurring task family, define what makes the tasks similar, collect a small batch, process it with the same setup, and record completed items, rework, waiting time, and missed urgency. Compare with the ordinary flow before expanding the batch.
entries.check_in: Did batching remove repeated setup without adding unacceptable delay, rework, or missed urgent work?

entries.title: Before You Commit to a Judgment, Consider the Opposite
entries.description: When a judgment matters and you already feel convinced, deliberately generate a plausible explanation, evidence pattern, or outcome that would point the other way. Use it as a bias check, not as a rule to distrust every conclusion.
entries.action: Write your current conclusion in one sentence. Then ask: what evidence, mechanism, or alternative explanation could make the opposite conclusion reasonable? Generate a concrete alternative rather than telling yourself to be objective. Check whether your decision would change if that alternative were true. Use this on decisions where biased assimilation or one-sided hypothesis testing is a real risk; do not turn it into endless doubt about routine choices.
entries.check_in: What plausible disconfirming case did I generate, and did it reveal a missing fact, a weak assumption, or no meaningful reason to change course?

entries.title: Benchmark AI on the Task Before You Trust the Workflow
entries.description: AI performance is uneven across tasks that can look similarly difficult. Before redesigning a workflow around a model, run it on representative cases, score the outputs against a human-defined standard, and identify where human review is still mandatory.
entries.action: Choose a small sample containing easy, ordinary, and awkward cases. Define what counts as acceptable before running the model. Compare AI output with the source or a trusted human result, record failure patterns, and decide which cases can be assisted, which need review, and which should stay human-first.
entries.check_in: Do I know the cases where AI is reliable enough to help and the cases where its polished answer should not be trusted?

entries.title: Boost Recall with Full Lists
entries.description: To remember all items: - Avoid splitting lists: Keep the whole list in view when reviewing. - Use categories: Organize items into groups to make them easier to recall. - Quiz yourself: After reviewing, cover the list and test yourself on all the items. Example: When memorizing a grocery list, don’t focus only on part of it—review the entire list.
entries.action: To remember all items: - Avoid splitting lists: Keep the whole list in view when reviewing. - Use categories: Organize items into groups to make them easier to recall. - Quiz yourself: After reviewing, cover the list and test yourself on all the items. Example: When memorizing a grocery list, don’t focus only on part of it—review the entire list.
entries.check_in: Check in when you use a full-list approach to improve recall.

entries.title: Break Free from Stereotypes
entries.description: To reduce stereotypical bias: - Pause and question: Before making assumptions, ask yourself, “What evidence do I have?” - Focus on individuals: Get to know people beyond labels and categories. - Seek diverse perspectives: Actively listen to stories and views different from your own. Example: Instead of assuming someone’s skills based on their background, ask them about their experiences directly.

Example: Instead of assuming someone’s skills based on their background, ask them about their experiences directly.
entries.check_in: Check in when you challenge and replace stereotypical assumptions.

entries.title: Build a QA Checklist from Real Failure Modes
entries.description: Turn a recurring QA task into a short checklist with clear expected results, exception handling, an owner, and a revision step when reality exposes a missing check.
entries.action: Choose one recurring QA activity, list the failure modes that would matter, turn each necessary check into an action plus expected result, define what to capture when the result differs, run the checklist on real work, and revise it when a new recurring miss appears.
entries.check_in: Which check changed the release or review decision, which item was ambiguous, and what should be added, removed, or rewritten before the next run?

entries.title: Build a Support Map Around Specific Needs
entries.description: Map the kinds of support you sometimes need, identify appropriate people or communities for each kind, make specific requests that are easy to decline, and protect reciprocity and boundaries.
entries.action: Write down one current need, decide what kind of help would actually be useful, identify a person or community that is appropriate for that request, ask specifically and make declining easy, respect the answer, and record whether you need a different resource or a different kind of help next time.
entries.check_in: Was the request specific and appropriate, was the other person's boundary clear, and do I need to change the ask, the resource, or my own next action?

entries.title: Build an AI-Assisted Question Bank You Can Verify
entries.description: Use AI to draft varied practice questions from material you already have, verify every answer against the source, and keep only questions that test the knowledge you actually need.
entries.action: Choose a source you need to learn, ask AI for questions covering definitions, explanations, comparisons, application and error cases, verify every answer against the source, remove ambiguous or unsupported items, and practice from the cleaned bank.
entries.check_in: Which questions exposed a gap, which answers could not be verified, and what should be corrected or added before the next practice round?

entries.title: Build Toward a Weekly Movement Baseline
entries.description: Plan how ordinary walking, moderate activity, vigorous activity or strength work can fit your week. Adapt the plan to your abilities and medical guidance rather than forcing one routine.
entries.action: Look at the coming week, mark the activity you already do, then add realistic walking, moderate or vigorous activity, and strength sessions where they fit. Build gradually rather than treating the guideline as a one-day target.
entries.check_in: Does the plan fit your current ability, schedule and any guidance from your health professional? Adjust it rather than forcing a target that is inappropriate for you.

entries.title: Calibrate Task Estimates With Planned vs Actual Work
entries.description: Define a concrete deliverable, make an initial estimate, record what completion actually required, note the main source of difference, and use that local record when planning similar work again.
entries.action: Write the deliverable and important assumptions, make an estimate that includes the work you currently know about, complete or reassess the task, record the actual conditions and the main reason for any difference, then consult that record before estimating similar work again.
entries.check_in: What did I estimate, what actually happened, what caused the largest difference, and what will I change in the next comparable estimate?

entries.title: Challenge Assumed Similarities
entries.description: When interacting with others: - Ask: "What’s unique about this person’s perspective or experience?" - Listen actively: Avoid projecting your own traits or beliefs onto them. - Reflect: Notice when you assume similarities without evidence and correct yourself. Example: Don’t assume a coworker has the same work style as you; ask about their preferences and needs.
entries.action: When interacting with others: - Ask: "What’s unique about this person’s perspective or experience?" - Listen actively: Avoid projecting your own traits or beliefs onto them. - Reflect: Notice when you assume similarities without evidence and correct yourself. Example: Don’t assume a coworker has the same work style as you; ask about their preferences and needs.
entries.check_in: Check in when you actively avoid assuming someone is just like you.

entries.title: Challenge Hindsight Bias
entries.description: When reviewing past events: - List surprises: Note things that were unexpected at the time. - Avoid ‘should haves’: Focus on decisions made with the information you had then. - Compare predictions: Look back at what you expected versus what happened. Example: After a project, review what you thought would happen and compare it to the outcome.

Example: After a project, review what you thought would happen and compare it to the outcome.
entries.check_in: Check in when you identify a moment where hindsight altered your perspective.

entries.title: Challenge the Consensus
entries.description: In group discussions: - Ask questions: "Have we considered other perspectives?" - Encourage dissent: Create a safe space for alternative viewpoints. - Pause before deciding: Suggest taking time to explore overlooked options. Example: Before agreeing with a team’s rushed decision, propose reviewing potential risks and alternatives.

Example: Before agreeing with a team’s rushed decision, propose reviewing potential risks and alternatives.
entries.check_in: Check in when you challenge groupthink and push for diverse perspectives.

entries.title: Check a Relevant Baseline Before Interpreting One Case
entries.description: For an ordinary data-informed decision, define the relevant reference class, find a comparable baseline, inspect its scope and denominator, then combine that general context with the facts that are specific to the case.
entries.action: State the decision, define the reference class, find a baseline with a clear denominator and scope, check whether it is comparable to the current case, add the case-specific information that genuinely differs, and keep the conclusion tentative when the baseline or fit is weak.
entries.check_in: What reference class did I use, where did its baseline come from, how comparable is it to this case, and which case-specific fact could justify departing from it?

entries.title: Check a Streak Before Treating It as a Pattern
entries.description: When a short streak looks meaningful, record the complete observation window and denominator, compare the cluster with the broader history, check whether measurement or operating conditions changed, and avoid changing a plan solely because the sequence looks striking.
entries.action: Record what happened, the full period or set you are looking at, and the denominator behind the visible cluster. Compare it with the earlier history when available, note any change in measurement or operating conditions, identify plausible alternative explanations, and choose whether to act, gather more information or keep the current plan.
entries.check_in: What streak caught my attention, what is the full denominator and observation window, what changed in the context, and would I make the same decision if the sequence looked less visually striking?

entries.title: Check Blame Bias
entries.description: When assigning blame: - Pause: Ask, "Am I blaming more because the outcome was worse?" - Separate outcome from intent: Focus on actions, not just consequences. - Avoid personal filters: Check if you’re influenced by similarities to the victim. Example: In a car accident case, avoid assigning more blame just because the damage was severe.
entries.action: When assigning blame: - Pause: Ask, "Am I blaming more because the outcome was worse?" - Separate outcome from intent: Focus on actions, not just consequences. - Avoid personal filters: Check if you’re influenced by similarities to the victim. Example: In a car accident case, avoid assigning more blame just because the damage was severe.
entries.check_in: Check in when you assess blame without being influenced by severity or personal connections.

entries.title: Check Email in Deliberate Windows Instead of Continuously
entries.description: If constant inbox checking fragments your day, test a few deliberate email windows and close the inbox between them. Match the schedule to real response expectations rather than copying a fixed number from a study.
entries.action: Choose a small number of email windows that still meet the real response expectations of your work and personal life. Close or hide the inbox between those windows and disable nonessential email alerts. Keep a separate urgent channel for issues that genuinely cannot wait. Do not treat three checks per day as a universal rule; that was the experimental condition, not an optimized schedule.
entries.check_in: Was my day less stressful or fragmented, did I miss anything genuinely time-sensitive, and did I compensate by manually reopening the inbox anyway?

entries.title: Check the Operating Context Before Reusing a Decision
entries.description: Before applying a familiar solution, state what changed, identify the people and system constraints that matter, separate verified facts from assumptions, and choose a reversible next step when important context is still missing.
entries.action: State the decision, note what changed since the comparable case, list the concrete constraints and stakeholders that affect execution, mark assumptions separately from verified facts, and choose a reversible next step or clarification when a missing condition could change the choice.
entries.check_in: What changed, which constraint matters now, what am I assuming rather than verifying, and what is the smallest next step that fits the current context?

entries.title: Check Whether a Streak Changes the Next Event
entries.description: Before acting on a streak, identify whether earlier outcomes can change the next event and use a pre-defined decision rule rather than a story about what is due.
entries.action: Describe the next event and the recent streak. Ask what carries information or state from earlier outcomes into the next one. If there is no connection, ignore the streak and use the same probability or decision rule. If a connection may exist, identify the relevant state and gather that information. Use a pre-defined stop rule for repeated high-cost decisions.
entries.check_in: What connection did I identify between past and next events, and did my action follow the rule or merely the feeling that an outcome was due?

entries.title: Check Whether Familiarity Is Driving a Low-Stakes Choice
entries.description: For an ordinary low-stakes choice, name the familiar default, state the criterion that matters, compare one viable alternative, and keep or change the default for a concrete reason rather than novelty alone.
entries.action: Name the default, write the criterion that matters, identify one viable alternative, compare the two on that criterion and any important constraint, then keep the default or try the alternative for a stated reason. Use this only for ordinary low-stakes choices.
entries.check_in: What was the default, what criterion mattered, what alternative did I compare, and why did I keep or change the choice?

entries.title: Check Who, What, Where, When, Why, and How
entries.description: Before an important operational message, check whether the reader has the people, action, place, timing, reason, and next-step details they actually need.
entries.action: Review an important operational message using six questions: Who? What? Where? When? Why? How? Add only the missing details the reader needs to act, then send the shortest version that is still clear.
entries.check_in: Could the reader act without guessing, and did I include any detail that was unnecessary or sensitive?

entries.title: Choose Resources for the Next Concrete Step
entries.description: Start from the output or decision you need, choose the resource that best fits that next step, check authority, freshness, licensing and security where relevant, test the smallest useful use, then keep, defer or archive it.
entries.action: Name the output or decision you need, compare candidate resources on direct relevance and usability, check authority, freshness, licensing, privacy and security where they matter, try the smallest useful interaction, and record whether to keep, defer or archive the resource.
entries.check_in: What next step was this resource meant to support, did it fit that job, what constraint did I verify, and should I keep using it, defer it or archive it?

entries.title: Choose Up to Three Priority Outcomes for the Day
entries.description: Choose a small set of outcomes that deserves protected attention today, define what done means, and move the rest to a visible backlog instead of pretending every task is equally urgent.
entries.action: Review today's deadlines, dependencies, and available capacity; choose up to three outcomes that most deserve progress; define what done means for each; reserve appropriate time where possible; place other tasks in a visible backlog; and re-plan explicitly when genuinely urgent work changes the day.
entries.check_in: Which priority outcomes moved today, what changed the plan, and what should be carried forward rather than silently added to tomorrow?

entries.title: Clarify Probabilities
entries.description: To improve judgment: - Break it down: Divide events into clear, mutually exclusive parts. - Add them up: Compare individual probabilities to the total likelihood. - Check your math: Avoid underestimating by verifying if the sum makes sense. Example: When assessing risks for a project, split them into categories (e.g., budget, time, resources) and evaluate each separately.

entries.title: Clear the ‘Tip of the Tongue’ Block
entries.description: To unblock stuck memories: - Relax: Take deep breaths and stop stressing over the word or idea. - Use hints: Think of related words, phrases, or contexts. - Distract yourself: Do something else for a while; it often pops up later. Example: If you can’t recall a name, focus on where you met the person or other details about them.

entries.title: Combat the Continued Influence Effect
entries.description: When dealing with misinformation: - Fact-check: Verify the source of any information before accepting it. - Mentally replace: Once corrected, actively focus on the updated information. - Repeat the truth: Reinforce the correct version to overwrite the false one. Example: If a rumor about a coworker turns out false, remind yourself of the actual facts whenever you think about them.

entries.title: Combat the Google Effect
entries.description: To reduce dependency on search engines: - Write things down: Jot key facts in a notebook or app. - Memorize essentials: Focus on learning critical knowledge by heart. - Quiz yourself: Test what you know without looking it up. Example: Instead of Googling a frequent recipe, memorize it and practice making it.

entries.check_in: Check in when you recall something without needing to look it up online.

entries.title: Comfortable Breathing Reset
entries.description: Use a few comfortable, unforced breaths as a brief pause before deciding what to do next. Skip counts that create strain or dizziness.
entries.action: Sit or stand comfortably, let your breathing slow without forcing a count, take a few easy breaths, and then return attention to one concrete next action.
entries.check_in: Did the pause help you feel more settled and able to choose the next action? Stop if breathing feels uncomfortable or light-headed.

entries.title: Comfortable Diaphragmatic Breathing
entries.description: Try a few slow, comfortable breaths while noticing the abdomen move. Keep the exercise easy, stop if it feels uncomfortable, and do not use it instead of medical care.
entries.action: Sit or lie in a comfortable position, let the breath slow without forcing a count, notice the abdomen rise and fall, and stop after a few easy cycles or whenever you prefer.
entries.check_in: Did the exercise feel comfortable and leave you ready for the next ordinary action? Stop if you feel dizzy, short of breath, distressed, or otherwise unwell.

entries.title: Compare a Condition With the Same Condition Plus Another Requirement
entries.description: When one option is A and another is A plus an additional condition B, write the two event sets explicitly and check their logical relationship before letting the more detailed description seem more likely.
entries.action: Identify condition A, identify the additional condition B, write the compound event as A-and-B, and check whether every compound case is already included among the A cases. If so, do not rank the compound event above A merely because the added detail makes the story feel more specific.
entries.check_in: What was A, what extra condition did B add, is every A-and-B case already an A case, and did the detailed wording change my initial ranking?

entries.title: Compare Two Approaches and Learn From the Result
entries.description: When a decision is reversible, compare two approaches around one clear question, keep the outcome you care about visible, and avoid treating a tiny informal comparison as statistical proof.
entries.action: Choose one reversible decision, define what you want to learn, compare two approaches as fairly as you can, and record the outcome before deciding what to try next. Use proper experimental design when the result needs statistical confidence.
entries.check_in: What changed between the two approaches, what outcome did I observe, and is the evidence strong enough to act or only strong enough to suggest another test?

entries.title: Connect a General Point to a Concrete Example
entries.description: State the general point, add a concrete example or observable detail that belongs to it, connect the example back to the point, and remove specifics that do not help the audience understand the message or next action.
entries.action: Write the main point in plain language, choose an example, observation, step or verified figure that illustrates it, explain the connection in one sentence, and remove details that do not change understanding or action. If you began with a detail, reverse the sequence by stating the broader point it supports.
entries.check_in: What is the general point, which concrete detail makes it easier to understand, what does that detail show here, and which specifics can be removed without changing the meaning?

entries.title: Counterexample Check
entries.description: When a statement uses words such as always, never, everyone, or nothing, look for one genuine exception before treating it as a rule.
entries.action: Write the absolute statement, underline the universal word, and find one genuine case where the statement does not hold. Then rewrite the claim more precisely.
entries.check_in: Did the counterexample change the claim, or was the original statement already precise enough to survive the check?

entries.title: Create a Clear Handoff Between Two Activities
entries.description: Use a short, ordinary handoff at a recurring boundary—such as work to personal time—to record what is unfinished, reset the environment, and make the first action of the next activity explicit.
entries.action: Choose one recurring transition, write down any unfinished item that must be resumed later, perform one simple closing action in the environment, name the first action of the next activity, then leave the handoff alone unless it proves useful enough to repeat.
entries.check_in: What did I close, what did I preserve for later, what is the first action in the next mode, and did this handoff reduce avoidable switching friction?

entries.title: Decision Calibration Journal
entries.description: Before an uncertain decision, record your expectation, confidence, and key assumption. Later compare them with the outcome and update how you make similar choices.
entries.action: Before a meaningful uncertain choice, write the expected outcome, how confident you are in plain language, and the assumption that matters most. Revisit the note after the outcome is clear.
entries.check_in: Which assumption held, which one failed, and what would you change in a similar decision next time?

entries.title: Decompose a Hard Problem with TRIZ-Inspired Contradictions
entries.description: Describe the unwanted result, expose the trade-off or contradiction, split the system into parts, and check a change that removes a constraint instead of merely optimizing around it.
entries.action: State the unwanted outcome, map the main parts and interactions, write the trade-off as two requirements that appear to conflict, generate separation or redesign options, choose a reversible check, and record which assumption or constraint changed.
entries.check_in: What contradiction did I expose, what separation or redesign did I check, and did it remove the conflict or only move it elsewhere?

entries.title: Deepen Memory with Levels of Processing
entries.description: To remember more effectively: - Think deeply: Relate new info to something personal or meaningful. - Visualize: Picture concepts or create mental stories about them. - Engage actively: Rephrase or discuss what you’re learning. Example: Instead of memorizing “photosynthesis,” think about how it powers the food you eat and describe it to a friend.
entries.action: To remember more effectively: - Think deeply: Relate new info to something personal or meaningful. - Visualize: Picture concepts or create mental stories about them. - Engage actively: Rephrase or discuss what you’re learning. Example: Instead of memorizing “photosynthesis,” think about how it powers the food you eat and describe it to a friend.
entries.check_in: Check in when you use deeper processing techniques to improve memory.
keywords: Deepen Memory with Levels of Processing

entries.title: Deliberate Attention Switching with Everyday Sounds
entries.description: Use several neutral sounds around you to practice deliberately selecting one sound, switching to another, and then noticing several at once. Treat this as an attention-flexibility drill, not a treatment for worry, anxiety, or another condition.
entries.action: Find a safe place with several ordinary sounds. Attend closely to one sound without needing to block the others. Deliberately switch to a second and then a third sound. Finish by broadening attention so several sounds can be noticed together. Keep the exercise brief and stop when you choose.
entries.check_in: Could you intentionally select, switch, and broaden attention? Record the skill you practiced, not whether worry or another symptom changed.

entries.title: Distinguish Intent from Accident
entries.description: When evaluating actions: - Ask: "Could this have been an accident or unintentional?" - Look for patterns: One mistake doesn’t indicate intent—watch for repeated behavior. - Check your biases: Avoid assuming intent without solid evidence. Example: If a coworker forgets to share notes, consider if it was an oversight rather than deliberate exclusion.

entries.check_in: Check in when you distinguish between intentional and accidental actions.

entries.title: Do a Short Desk Reset
entries.description: Set a timer for 2 minutes and tidy up your workspace. Put away unnecessary items and clear some space for your tasks.
entries.action: Set a short timer and tidy one small part of your workspace. Make only obvious moves, then stop before tidying turns into a larger task.
entries.check_in: Is the workspace easier to use now, and did I stop before tidying became a new form of procrastination?
keywords: Set a Timer for a 2-Minute Cleanup

entries.title: Do Active Listening Exercises
entries.description: Practice active listening by summarizing and repeating back what the other person has said to confirm understanding.
entries.action: In one conversation, wait until the other person finishes a thought, paraphrase the main point in your own words, invite correction, and ask one open question before offering advice or changing the topic.
entries.check_in: Did I summarize before responding? Was my summary accepted or corrected, and what did the correction teach me?

entries.title: Draft Professional Writing with AI, Then Take Back the Edit
entries.description: For routine professional writing, give AI the purpose, audience, constraints, and source facts, ask for a draft, then revise it yourself. Controlled evidence supports productivity gains for some professional writing tasks, not automatic accuracy or judgment.
entries.action: Provide the audience, goal, source facts, must-include points, and constraints. Ask for one draft. Compare it with the source material, remove invented details, restore your own judgment and voice, and send only the version you can defend without the model in the room.
entries.check_in: Did AI reduce drafting time without introducing claims, tone, or commitments I would not have written myself?

entries.title: Embrace Outsider Ideas
entries.description: When evaluating external ideas: - Ask: "Is this idea or product effective, regardless of where it came from?" - Compare: Assess its potential objectively against internal solutions. - Collaborate: Consider how external knowledge might complement your existing methods. Example: Your team resists using an external tool because it’s not developed in-house. Challenge this by focusing on its benefits and efficiency.

entries.check_in: Check in when you adopt or explore an external idea that adds value.

entries.title: End on a High Note
entries.description: To create great memories: - Finish strong: End tasks or experiences with something positive. - Celebrate small wins: After completing a tough task, reward yourself with something enjoyable. - Pause to reflect: Take a moment to focus on the highlights before ending your day. Example: After a meeting, share a positive takeaway with your team to leave a good impression.

entries.check_in: Check in when you focus on the best parts and how you wrap up experiences.

entries.title: Evaluate Options Against Fixed Criteria Before Comparing Them
entries.description: Define the must-have criteria first, inspect each option against the same criteria, record unknowns separately, and compare survivors only after the individual evaluations are complete.
entries.action: Write the must-have constraints and relevant preferences before opening the comparison, evaluate each option against that same list, mark missing information as unknown rather than pass or fail, remove options that clearly violate a must-have, and compare the remaining trade-offs only after the individual evaluations are recorded.
entries.check_in: Did I keep the same criteria across options, which unknown could still change the result, and which remaining trade-off actually matters?

entries.title: Expect the Unexpected
entries.description: When predicting trends: - Ask yourself: "Could there be sudden changes or breaks in this trend?" - Prepare for shifts: Always consider outliers and unexpected events in planning. - Look for weak signals: Early signs of change can help you adapt quickly. Example: A stock steadily rising? Plan for a downturn just as much as for continued growth.

entries.title: Explain One Idea with an Analogy and Its Limit
entries.description: Compare an unfamiliar idea with something familiar, state the matching point, name where the comparison stops and ask the listener to restate the idea.
entries.action: Write the idea you need to explain. Choose a familiar comparison, map only the important relationship, add one boundary sentence and ask the listener to restate the original idea. Revise the analogy if the restatement keeps the wrong detail.
entries.check_in: Could the listener restate the intended idea, and which part of the analogy clarified or distorted it?

entries.title: Explain What You Just Learned in Your Own Words
entries.description: After a meaningful chunk of digital learning, pause and explain the idea, relationship, or step in your own words, then compare with the source and correct gaps. Meta-analytic evidence supports self-explanation in digital learning, with meaningful variation across contexts and material types.
entries.action: Study a manageable chunk, then look away from the explanation and produce a brief self-explanation: what the idea means, why a step follows, how it connects to what you already know, or when it would apply. Compare your explanation with the source, identify one gap or error, and revise it. Use the prompts that fit the material; do not turn every paragraph into a compulsory monologue.
entries.check_in: Can I explain the idea accurately enough to reconstruct the key relationship or step, and what did I have to correct after checking the source?

entries.title: Explore Childhood Amnesia
entries.description: To recall early memories: - Use triggers: Look at photos or listen to music from your early years. - Ask family: Talk to relatives about events you may have forgotten. - Write it down: Jot down fragments of memories as they surface. Example: A photo of a birthday party might help you recall more about the event.

entries.check_in: Check in when you recall an early memory with the help of a trigger or conversation.

entries.title: Extract a Table with AI, Then Sample-Check the Rows
entries.description: For repeated unstructured text you are allowed to process, ask AI to extract a fixed schema, include the source span for each row, and flag uncertainty. Then sample-check rows and fully verify fields that drive money, access, compliance, or other high-cost actions.
entries.action: Define the columns and allowed values before extraction. Ask the model to return null rather than guess, preserve a source snippet or locator for each row, and flag ambiguous cases. Check a random sample plus all high-impact rows against the original text before using the result downstream.
entries.check_in: Do I know the observed extraction error rate well enough for the consequence of the next step?

entries.title: Focus on Best Odds
entries.description: When making decisions with probabilities: - Stick to the best choice: Pick the option with the highest likelihood of success, even if it feels repetitive. - Avoid overthinking: Don’t try to "balance" probabilities—maximize them instead. - Track outcomes: Note what works best over time to reinforce smarter decisions. Example: Choosing between two investments? Opt for the one with higher consistent returns, even if less exciting.

entries.title: Focus on the Bigger Picture
entries.description: When working with metrics: - Ask yourself: "Is this measure representing the actual goal, or has it become the goal?" - Revisit the strategy: Ensure you understand the broader objective the metric supports. - Avoid tunnel vision: Regularly check if actions are aligned with the ultimate goal. Example: Focusing solely on sales numbers? Balance them with customer satisfaction to maintain long-term success.

entries.title: Give AI a Rubric and Ask for Specific Critique
entries.description: For a draft you own, give AI the purpose and a short rubric, ask it to point to specific places that miss the criteria, then decide which suggestions actually improve the work. Use critique as input, not as an automatic rewrite command.
entries.action: Write three to six criteria that describe a good result. Give the model the draft and rubric, ask for evidence from the draft for each criticism, and request no rewrite on the first pass. Triage the feedback, then make the changes you agree with.
entries.check_in: Did the critique point to observable gaps in the draft, or mostly produce generic advice I could paste onto any text?

entries.title: Goal Journal Review
entries.description: Use a short goal journal to capture what you planned, what actually happened, what got in the way, and one adjustment for the next attempt.
entries.action: After a meaningful work session or at a regular review point, write four short lines: what I intended, what happened, what helped or blocked me, and what I will change next.
entries.check_in: Did the journal produce one concrete adjustment, or did it become another place to write without changing anything?

entries.title: Guard Against Misinformation
entries.description: To protect memory: - Verify info: Check facts before trusting new details about an event. - Write it down: Record key facts right after an event to lock them in. - Question changes: Be skeptical of info that seems to alter your original memory. Example: If you hear a new version of a story, cross-check it with your original notes or memory.

entries.check_in: Check in when you verify facts to prevent misinformation from altering your memory.

entries.title: Handle Long Lists: - Chunk It: Break the List into Smaller Groups of 3–5
entries.description: To handle long lists: - Chunk it: Break the list into smaller groups of 3–5 items. - Prioritize: Focus on the most important items first. - Use categories: Group similar items together to make them easier to remember. Example: When shopping, group items like fruits, dairy, and snacks into separate categories.

entries.title: Handle Resistance Calmly
entries.description: When facing reactance: - Reframe requests: Offer choices instead of commands to reduce resistance. - Empathize: Understand the other person’s need for autonomy and validate their feelings. - Negotiate: Collaborate on solutions that respect their freedom. Example: Instead of saying, "You must do this now," say, "Would you prefer to tackle this now or after lunch?"

entries.title: Harness Focus: - Start Small: Begin a Task, Even If You Can’t Finish It
entries.description: To harness focus: - Start small: Begin a task, even if you can’t finish it right away. - Use checkpoints: Pause at natural stopping points to keep motivation. - Let it linger: Use the tension of an unfinished task to stay motivated. Example: Write the first sentence of an email or presentation to make it easier to continue later.

entries.title: Improve Memory: - Use Visuals: Add Images to Your Notes or Presentations

Example: When learning vocabulary, draw a quick picture next to each word to make it easier to recall.

entries.check_in: Check in when you use pictures to strengthen your memory of information.

entries.title: In a Group, Write Down Ideas and Pass Them Around for Others to Build
entries.description: In a group, write down ideas and pass them around for others to build on.
entries.action: Give the group one clear question, let everyone write ideas silently, pass the ideas to another person to add or change them, and delay discussion until the group has built several options.
entries.check_in: Did everyone get a chance to contribute before discussion? Which idea became more useful after another person built on it, and what should the group test next?

entries.title: Judge a Commitment by What Comes Next
entries.description: When past time, money, or effort is dominating a continuation decision, separate what cannot be recovered and compare realistic future costs, benefits, constraints, and alternatives.
entries.action: Name the decision. Separate unrecoverable past cost from future cost. List the realistic benefit of continuing, the best alternative use of the same resources, and any obligation or switching cost that genuinely exists now. Then choose stop, continue, change, or gather one missing fact.
entries.check_in: If I were deciding from today forward, what future cost and benefit would justify continuing, and what alternative am I giving up?

entries.title: Judge Actions, Not Outcomes
entries.description: When assessing morality: - Focus on intent: Ask, "What was their intention, regardless of the outcome?" - Separate luck from action: Consider how chance influenced the result. - Be fair: Avoid overpraising or blaming based on outcomes alone. Example: If someone saves a life by chance, their intent to help matters as much as the lucky outcome.

entries.check_in: Check in when you evaluate actions based on intent rather than results.

entries.title: Judge Each Option Against the Same Criteria
entries.description: Define the decision criteria before comparing options, assess each option on its own and only then compare the results.
entries.action: State the outcome and non-negotiables. Review each option separately using the same short criteria and note pass, unclear or fail. Compare only after the separate assessments are complete. Recheck any choice that depends mainly on the previous option looking unusually good or bad.
entries.check_in: Would I make the same choice if this option appeared first, and which criterion actually supports the decision?

entries.title: Judge Individuals, Not Groups
entries.description: When evaluating groups: - Ask yourself: "Am I judging the group based on one person’s actions?" - Separate individuals: Focus on specific behaviors or contributions, not stereotypes. - Avoid sweeping judgments: Base evaluations on evidence, not generalizations. Example: If one team member underperforms, don’t assume the whole team is inefficient.

Example: If one team member underperforms, don’t assume the whole team is inefficient.
entries.check_in: Check in when you focus on individuals instead of generalizing about groups.

entries.title: Keep a Work Wins Log You Can Reuse
entries.description: Record completed work, solved problems, decisions, useful contributions and recoveries in a compact log so you can retrieve concrete examples for reviews, resumes, proposals, retrospectives and planning.
entries.action: After a meaningful piece of work, add a short entry with the situation, your contribution, the concrete result or current state, and one or two tags. During a review, retrieve entries that match the purpose and verify any figures or claims before reusing them.
entries.check_in: What changed, what did I contribute, what detail will I need later, and is the entry specific enough to reuse without exaggeration?

entries.title: Leave a Ready-to-Resume Note Before You Switch Tasks
entries.description: When you must leave unfinished work, capture where you stopped, the next concrete action, and one critical restart detail before switching. The goal is a cleaner return, not eliminating every cost of interruption.
entries.action: Use this only when unfinished work is about to be interrupted or deliberately parked. Before switching, capture three pieces of information in whatever format fits the task: your current state, the next concrete action, and one critical detail or open question that would otherwise have to be reconstructed. Then switch. When you return, read the note and start from the recorded next action rather than re-scanning the entire task.
entries.check_in: When I returned, could I identify the next action quickly, or did I still have to reconstruct the task from scratch?

entries.title: Leave Useful Feedback
entries.description: Write feedback that separates what happened, why it mattered to you, and what change would make the experience better.
entries.action: Describe one concrete thing that worked or failed, explain the effect it had on your task, and add one specific suggestion if you have one.
entries.check_in: Could the recipient understand what happened and what might improve without guessing what you meant?

entries.title: Let AI Draft Routine Replies, Keep the Human on the Conversation
entries.description: For repetitive support or service messages, AI can propose a response from the case facts and approved guidance while the human checks diagnosis, policy, tone, and the actual next step. Large-scale field evidence supports gains in one customer-support setting, especially for less experienced workers.
entries.action: Provide only information you are allowed to share, plus the customer question and approved policy or knowledge source. Ask for a concise draft. Check that it answers the real issue, does not invent policy or status, and gives the correct next action before sending.
entries.check_in: Did the suggestion save wording effort while leaving the human more attentive to the customer's actual problem?

entries.title: Leverage the Humor Effect
entries.description: To remember better: - Add humor: When studying or taking notes, include a funny phrase, drawing, or analogy. - Lighten the mood: Associate dry facts with jokes or funny stories. - Laugh it off: Share what you’ve learned in a humorous way with others. Example: To remember “photosynthesis,” picture a plant wearing sunglasses and sipping a smoothie!

Example: To remember “photosynthesis,” picture a plant wearing sunglasses and sipping a smoothie!
entries.check_in: Check in when you use humor to make something memorable.

entries.title: Look Beyond Morals
entries.description: When assessing outcomes: - Pause: Ask yourself, "Could societal factors have contributed here?" - Contextualize: Consider external influences like environment, resources, or circumstances. - Avoid blame: Shift from moral judgment to understanding. Example: If someone misses a deadline, think about workload or system issues rather than assuming laziness.
