Example: If someone misses a deadline, think about workload or system issues rather than assuming laziness.
entries.check_in: Check in when you assess situations without jumping to moral judgments.

entries.title: Make a Specific Repair Attempt After a Workable Conflict
entries.description: After a misunderstanding or conflict where it is safe to re-engage, make a specific repair attempt: name what you did, acknowledge the likely impact without arguing about intent, apologize for your part, offer a concrete corrective action, and invite the other person's view. Do not demand forgiveness or immediate reconciliation.
entries.action: Wait until you can speak without escalating. Name the specific action or words you are taking responsibility for. Acknowledge the impact as you understand it without using your intention to cancel the other person's experience. Apologize for your part without an 'if'. Offer one concrete repair or behavior change you can actually make, then ask how the other person sees it. Listen to the answer. Do not require forgiveness, agreement, or immediate trust in return.
entries.check_in: Did I own a specific part without defending it, offer a realistic repair, and give the other person room to respond or decline?

entries.title: Make Goal Progress Visible Instead of Guessing
entries.description: For a goal you are actively pursuing, choose one observable progress signal, record it at useful checkpoints, compare it with the target, and use the result to adjust the next action. Monitoring helps when it informs action; more tracking is not automatically better.
entries.action: Choose one goal where feedback can still change what you do. Pick one observable indicator that is close to the real outcome or behavior you care about. Record it at checkpoints that match the task, compare it with the target or previous checkpoint, and decide one adjustment. Prefer a small trace you will actually use over a dashboard full of decorative metrics.
entries.check_in: What changed in the progress signal, and what is the one next action that follows from that information?

entries.title: Make Key Info Stand Out
entries.description: To remember better: - Highlight differently: Use bold colors or symbols for key points. - Add uniqueness: Attach a quirky story or image to important details. - Group by importance: Separate standout items from general information. Example: If studying a list, underline or use bright markers on the most critical items.
entries.action: To remember better: - Highlight differently: Use bold colors or symbols for key points. - Add uniqueness: Attach a quirky story or image to important details. - Group by importance: Separate standout items from general information. Example: If studying a list, underline or use bright markers on the most critical items.
entries.check_in: Check in when you make key information stand out in your notes.

entries.title: Make Your Phone Less Visually Tempting with Grayscale
entries.description: If you want to spend less time on your phone, try switching the display to grayscale for a bounded trial. Treat it as friction against habitual use, not as a productivity, sleep, or mental-health upgrade.
entries.action: Enable grayscale on your phone and leave the rest of your normal setup alone for a bounded trial. Use the phone when you actually need it; the point is not abstinence. Notice whether automatic checking becomes less attractive. If color is important for navigation, accessibility, work, photos, or another real task, switch color back on for that task instead of treating grayscale as a purity test.
entries.check_in: Did my phone screen time or automatic checking change, and did I simply move the same distraction to another device?

entries.title: Master Your Perception of Time
entries.description: To manage time perception: - Practice calmness: Breathe deeply to slow things down when you feel rushed. - Focus intently: In critical moments, focus on one detail at a time to create clarity. - Review after action: Reflect on what happened to separate emotions from actual timing. Example: During a stressful meeting, focus on your breath and slow your response to regain control.
entries.action: To manage time perception: - Practice calmness: Breathe deeply to slow things down when you feel rushed. - Focus intently: In critical moments, focus on one detail at a time to create clarity. - Review after action: Reflect on what happened to separate emotions from actual timing. Example: During a stressful meeting, focus on your breath and slow your response to regain control.
entries.check_in: Check in when you regulate your sense of time under pressure.

entries.title: Match Demanding Work to Your Own High-Energy Windows
entries.description: Track when demanding work feels easier or harder for several normal days, protect a promising window for one important task, and keep the change only if your own results justify it.
entries.action: For several ordinary workdays, note your perceived energy and the kind of work you were doing at a few points in the day, look for a repeatable high-energy window, place one demanding task there, protect the block from avoidable interruptions, and compare the result with your usual schedule.
entries.check_in: When did demanding work feel easiest today, what task did I place there, and did the scheduling change produce a result worth repeating?

entries.title: Match Feedback to the Revision Target
entries.description: When revising a student or learning-focused draft, decide whether the current pass targets surface features such as grammar and wording or deeper features such as ideas, organization, and coherence. Ask the reviewer to focus feedback on that target, revise at the same level, and use a separate pass when the other level also matters.
entries.action: Before asking for feedback on a student or learning-focused draft, choose the current revision target. Use a surface pass for grammar, spelling, wording, and similar features; use a deep pass for ideas, organization, coherence, or other meaning-level features. Tell the reviewer which level you want them to focus on, revise against that target, and run a separate pass if the other level also needs work.
entries.check_in: What was the revision target for this pass, and did the feedback actually help you revise at that level?

entries.title: Move Caffeine Earlier When Sleep Matters
entries.description: If caffeine may be reaching into the night, move the last dose earlier and reduce large late-day doses. A 2025 randomized crossover trial found that a single 400 mg dose disrupted several sleep measures even when taken many hours before bed; a small 100 mg dose did not show a significant effect at the tested timings. That is a reason to be dose-aware, not a license for one universal cutoff.
entries.action: For one or two weeks, note the time and rough amount of your last caffeine, your bedtime, and whether sleep onset, overnight restfulness, and next-day sleepiness are broadly better or worse. Start by moving the last large dose earlier or reducing it; do not deliberately take caffeine late just to test your tolerance.
entries.check_in: When was my last caffeine, roughly how much was it, and did sleep and next-day alertness look better, worse, or unchanged across several days?

entries.title: One Move, Several Benefits
entries.description: Look for one concrete action that advances two compatible priorities, then check that combining them does not make the action vague or overloaded.
entries.action: Name two priorities, brainstorm one concrete action that can serve both, and reject the combination if it makes either priority weaker or unclear.
entries.check_in: Did combining the priorities simplify the plan, or did it create a compromised task that serves neither one well?
keywords: Double Attack: Hit Multiple Goals at Once

entries.title: Organize Complex Information Around One Decision
entries.description: Define the audience and decision, group related material into labeled parts, put the main path in a useful order, and move supporting detail into linked layers instead of either flattening everything or presenting every detail at once.
entries.action: Name the primary audience and the decision or action they need to understand. Group related material by purpose, give each group a descriptive label, order the groups into a main path, and move supporting definitions, examples, calculations or source detail into a layer that remains easy to retrieve.
entries.check_in: What does the audience need to decide or do, which groups form the main path, what belongs in supporting detail, and can a reader find that detail when needed?

entries.title: Overcome Cross-Race Effect
entries.description: When meeting new people: - Focus on details: Pay attention to unique features, like hairstyle, clothing, or mannerisms. - Make connections: Associate the person with an activity or place to reinforce recognition. - Practice mindfulness: Avoid rushing interactions—give yourself time to observe. Example: If you meet someone at a conference, link their face to a topic they discussed.
entries.action: When meeting new people: - Focus on details: Pay attention to unique features, like hairstyle, clothing, or mannerisms. - Make connections: Associate the person with an activity or place to reinforce recognition. - Practice mindfulness: Avoid rushing interactions—give yourself time to observe. Example: If you meet someone at a conference, link their face to a topic they discussed.
entries.check_in: Check in when you recognize someone accurately despite initial difficulties.

entries.title: Overcome Memory Inhibition
entries.description: To retrieve all items: - Rotate focus: Review all parts of a list instead of sticking to the first items. - Use triggers: Write down clues to jog your memory for the forgotten parts. - Repeat evenly: Go over the list multiple times without overemphasizing certain items. Example: When revising notes, review sections evenly instead of just re-reading the first few pages.
entries.action: To retrieve all items: - Rotate focus: Review all parts of a list instead of sticking to the first items. - Use triggers: Write down clues to jog your memory for the forgotten parts. - Repeat evenly: Go over the list multiple times without overemphasizing certain items. Example: When revising notes, review sections evenly instead of just re-reading the first few pages.
entries.check_in: Check in when you recover forgotten parts of a list by balancing your focus.

entries.title: Own Successes AND Failures
entries.description: When reflecting on outcomes: - Be honest: Ask, "What role did I really play in this success or failure?" - Balance: Acknowledge both personal effort and external factors. - Learn from mistakes: Use failures as opportunities to grow, not excuses to deflect. Example: If a project goes well, credit teamwork and planning, not just your input.
entries.action: When reflecting on outcomes: - Be honest: Ask, "What role did I really play in this success or failure?" - Balance: Acknowledge both personal effort and external factors. - Learn from mistakes: Use failures as opportunities to grow, not excuses to deflect. Example: If a project goes well, credit teamwork and planning, not just your input.
entries.check_in: Check in when you give a balanced account of your role in success or failure.

entries.title: Pair a Useful Task with Something You Genuinely Want
entries.description: Pair a beneficial activity that is easy to postpone with a compatible pleasure you already enjoy. Temptation bundling has field-experiment support for exercise, but it is not a universal habit formula and effects can fade.
entries.action: Choose one 'should' behavior that is useful but easy to delay and one 'want' experience that can happen at the same time without making the task worse. Examples might include a favorite audiobook during a walk or routine cardio, a preferred podcast while doing repetitive household work, or another compatible pairing. If you want a stronger commitment device, reserve that entertainment for the target activity. Keep the pairing safe: do not add absorbing media to driving, technical work, strength movements that require concentration, or any task where divided attention creates risk.
entries.check_in: Did the pairing make the useful activity easier to start or repeat, and did the reward stay enjoyable without damaging the quality or safety of the task?

entries.title: Pause a Heated Disagreement and Test One Claim
entries.description: Slow down a defensive exchange, restate the other person's claim, identify what could change either view and choose one concrete check or a respectful stopping point.
entries.action: Notice that you are defending rather than examining. Pause before replying. Restate the other person's claim in words they accept, then state your own position and uncertainty. Ask what information would change either view. Choose one concrete check, or stop when the exchange is no longer productive or safe.
entries.check_in: What claim did we clarify, what could change either view, and did we choose a check, revise a position or stop respectfully?

entries.title: Pause Before Acting on a High-Stress Urge
entries.description: When a situation is safe enough to pause, notice the urge to react, describe what is happening, choose a harmless short delay, and then reassess the next action. This is not full DBT or crisis care.
entries.action: Pause. Describe the situation in one factual sentence and name the action urge without judging it. Choose a harmless brief activity that creates time rather than escalating the situation. Then reassess what action is safest and most useful.
entries.check_in: Did you create a pause without making the situation worse, and what safe next action did you choose? Do not score success by whether the emotion disappeared.

entries.title: Pause Before Assuming Hostility
entries.description: When interpreting behavior: - Pause: Ask yourself, "Could this be unintentional or neutral?" - Clarify: If unsure, communicate and seek their perspective. - Reflect: Check if past experiences are influencing your assumptions. Example: If someone doesn’t reply to an email, consider they might be busy, not ignoring you.
entries.action: When interpreting behavior: - Pause: Ask yourself, "Could this be unintentional or neutral?" - Clarify: If unsure, communicate and seek their perspective. - Reflect: Check if past experiences are influencing your assumptions. Example: If someone doesn’t reply to an email, consider they might be busy, not ignoring you.
entries.check_in: Check in when you interpret behavior without immediately assuming hostility.

entries.title: Pause Long Enough to Notice a Good Moment
entries.description: When something genuinely pleasant is already happening, give it a little deliberate attention instead of rushing past it. This is a conservative savoring practice, not a rule to feel positive or reinterpret difficult experiences.
entries.action: Choose a positive experience that is already real: a good meal, a joke, a quiet walk, finishing useful work, music, a kind message, or another ordinary moment. For a short period, stop adding new input. Notice one or two concrete details and what makes the moment worth noticing. Then continue your day. Do not use the exercise to deny an unpleasant feeling or to manufacture gratitude for something that is not good.
entries.check_in: Did I actually stay with a positive experience for a moment, and did the practice feel useful, neutral, awkward, or forced?

entries.title: Plan Your Workday in Three Simple Blocks
entries.description: Split the day into a few broad work blocks and choose a small set of clear outcomes for each. Use three blocks and up to three tasks per block as a template, not a rule.
entries.action: Divide the workday into up to three broad blocks. Give each block one to three clear outcomes that fit the time you actually have. Replan when meetings, urgent work, or delays change the day.
entries.check_in: Did the blocks help me choose what mattered, and was any block overloaded, too vague, or too rigid?

entries.title: Practice Facing a Small Fear Gradually
entries.description: When facing a fear, remind yourself that you’re safe. Repeat phrases like, ‘I am safe,’ ‘This is just a feeling,’ or ‘I can handle this.’
entries.action: Choose one situation you avoid because it feels frightening but that is not actually dangerous. Break it into smaller steps, start with a manageable step, approach it gradually, and notice what happens rather than trying to force fear away with a required phrase or ritual.
entries.check_in: What step did I try, how difficult did it feel before and after, what did I learn, and what would be a sensible next step?

entries.title: Practice One Small Language Skill for a Short Session
entries.description: Use a short study session to practice one narrow language skill such as recalling a few words, listening to a short clip, or speaking a brief response. Ten minutes is a convenient starting point, not a required dose.
entries.action: Pick one narrow language task, such as reviewing a few phrases, listening to a short clip, reading a small passage, or recording a brief spoken answer. Practice for a short session and finish with one note about what to revisit next.
entries.check_in: What did I practice, what could I recall or understand without help, and what is the next small thing worth repeating?

entries.title: Protect Enough Sleep Opportunity and Track Daytime Function
entries.description: If your sleep is routinely short, protect a realistic window that gives you enough opportunity to sleep and observe simple trends in sleep timing and daytime alertness. Do not deliberately restrict sleep to search for an 'optimal' number or treat one bad night as a result.
entries.action: Choose a bedtime-to-wake window that fits your obligations and gives you a reasonable opportunity for enough sleep. For a week or two, record only a few things: roughly when you tried to sleep, when you got up, whether the night was unusually disrupted, and how alert or sleepy you felt during the day. Look for repeated patterns, not single-night scores. Change one practical constraint at a time, such as moving bedtime earlier when your current schedule routinely leaves too little time for sleep.
entries.check_in: Did I give myself enough opportunity to sleep, what did my actual sleep/wake pattern look like, and was daytime alertness broadly better, unchanged, or worse over several days?

entries.title: Question Authority
entries.description: When considering an opinion or advice: - Ask yourself: "Am I agreeing because of the person or because of the evidence?" - Check the facts: Verify the information independently, regardless of who said it. - Value expertise over titles: Focus on the actual knowledge or experience behind the opinion. Example: A senior manager gives advice—analyze the content, not just their title.
entries.action: When considering an opinion or advice: - Ask yourself: "Am I agreeing because of the person or because of the evidence?" - Check the facts: Verify the information independently, regardless of who said it. - Value expertise over titles: Focus on the actual knowledge or experience behind the opinion. Example: A senior manager gives advice—analyze the content, not just their title.
entries.check_in: Check in when you evaluate advice based on evidence, not authority.

entries.title: Question Big Causes for Big Events
entries.description: When faced with a big event: - Ask yourself: "Is there solid evidence for a big cause, or am I assuming it because the event is large?" - Break it down: Look at smaller, logical factors that might explain the event. - Challenge conspiracy thinking: Focus on verified sources and avoid overgeneralizing. Example: A major market crash? Analyze economic trends rather than assuming a single catastrophic cause.

entries.title: Question Data in New Contexts
entries.description: When using numerical data: - Ask yourself: "Does this data apply to this specific situation?" - Double-check assumptions: Ensure the numbers make sense in the new context. - Explore alternatives: Seek additional information before drawing conclusions. Example: Using an old formula for a new project? Verify if it fits the current conditions first.

Example: Using an old formula for a new project? Verify if it fits the current conditions first.
entries.check_in: Check in when you verify the relevance of data in a new context.

entries.title: Question Leading Suggestions
entries.description: To resist suggestibility: - Slow down: Reflect before accepting others’ suggestions as true. - Seek evidence: Verify claims rather than relying on someone’s framing. - Ask critical questions: “Is this my thought, or has it been influenced?” Example: If someone suggests a memory (“Remember when we all agreed?”), ask for details to confirm.

entries.check_in: Check in when you pause to question a suggestion instead of accepting it immediately.

entries.title: Question Purposeful Explanations
entries.description: When noticing a purpose in random events: - Ask yourself: "Is there any actual evidence of intention or design here?" - Consider randomness: Some things happen by chance without any goal behind them. - Separate cause from purpose: Look for causal explanations rather than assuming intent. Example: A storm ruined plans? Don’t assume it “happened for a reason”—explore natural causes instead.

entries.title: Question the Fairness Narrative
entries.description: When analyzing injustice: - Ask: "Is this outcome truly deserved, or am I rationalizing it?" - Empathize: Consider factors outside the victim’s control. - Acknowledge reality: The world isn’t always fair—avoid blaming victims. Example: If someone loses their job unexpectedly, avoid assuming they must have done something wrong.

entries.title: Reality Check Your Memories
entries.description: To avoid false memories: - Validate facts: Check with others involved or revisit records (emails, photos, notes). - Stay neutral: Avoid over-analyzing or trying too hard to recall—this can create distortions. - Ask questions: Reflect on whether your memory feels vivid or constructed. Example: Before insisting that an event happened a certain way, verify it with a trusted source.

entries.check_in: Check in when you fact-check a memory to confirm its accuracy.

entries.title: Record What Would Change a Belief
entries.description: Write a claim, the basis for your current view, the new information and the condition under which you would revise, narrow or suspend the belief.
entries.action: Choose one claim that affects a decision. Write its current basis and the new information separately. Check whether the information addresses the same claim and context. Choose a disposition: unchanged, less certain, revised, narrowed or unresolved. Record what additional information would change the disposition.
entries.check_in: What changed in the claim, its scope or my certainty, and what information would justify another update?

entries.title: Record What Would Change Your Confidence Before You Commit
entries.description: State your current confidence in plain language, record the main support and unknowns, name an observable fact that would change the judgment, then compare the expectation with what later happened and update future decisions accordingly.
entries.action: State the decision or prediction, label your confidence in ordinary language, list the strongest support and the most important unknown, name one observable condition that would make you update, then revisit the record when the outcome or new information becomes available.
entries.check_in: What did I expect, how confident was I, what would have changed my view, what actually happened, and what should I update next time?

entries.title: Reduce Egocentric Bias
entries.description: When recalling events: - Use evidence: Look at photos, reports, or other objective records of what happened. - Ask others: Gather perspectives from those who were there. - Reflect honestly: Recognize moments where your memory might exaggerate your role or success. Example: If you remember organizing a successful event, check with others to confirm your recollection.
entries.action: When recalling events: - Use evidence: Look at photos, reports, or other objective records of what happened. - Ask others: Gather perspectives from those who were there. - Reflect honestly: Recognize moments where your memory might exaggerate your role or success. Example: If you remember organizing a successful event, check with others to confirm your recollection.
entries.check_in: Check in when you adjust your memory to reflect reality, not ego.

entries.title: Rehearse a Difficult Conversation with AI Before the Real One
entries.description: Before a difficult but ordinary conversation, use AI to role-play several plausible reactions, practise a concise opening, and identify points where you may become unclear or defensive. Treat the simulation as rehearsal, not as a model of the other person's mind.
entries.action: State the goal, your opening, and relevant context without unnecessary private detail. Ask AI to play a neutral, skeptical, and confused counterpart. Practise responding with facts, boundaries, and questions. Write one shorter opening after the rehearsal and use that in the real conversation if it still fits.
entries.check_in: Am I better prepared to listen and respond, or did I start treating the simulated person's reaction as a prediction?

entries.title: Rehearse One Real Language Scenario
entries.description: Choose a real low-risk interaction in the language you are learning, prepare the minimum useful phrases plus a repair phrase, rehearse likely turns, try the interaction when appropriate, and update the phrase set from what was difficult.
entries.action: Define the scenario and desired outcome, write the core request or response, add likely follow-up phrases and one repair phrase for misunderstanding, rehearse both sides aloud, use the interaction when appropriate, and update the phrase set from the point where you hesitated or needed clarification.
entries.check_in: Which scenario did I rehearse, where did the interaction become difficult, which phrase or listening cue should I add, and what can I reuse next time?

entries.title: Remember Better: - Create Your Own Notes: Instead of Copying, Rephrase in Your Own
entries.description: To remember better: - Create your own notes: Instead of copying, rephrase in your own words. - Teach someone else: Explaining ideas reinforces your understanding. - Summarize: Generate key points from what you learn and write them down. Example: After a meeting, jot down what you’ve learned in your own words to solidify your memory.

Example: After a meeting, jot down what you’ve learned in your own words to solidify your memory.
entries.check_in: Check in when you generate your own version of a concept to enhance recall.

entries.title: Remember Better: - Listen and Repeat: Say Key Points Aloud After Hearing Them
entries.description: To remember better: - Listen and repeat: Say key points aloud after hearing them. - Mix modalities: Write down spoken info or speak aloud written notes. - Review audio: Record important notes and listen back later. Example: After a meeting, record a summary of key points and listen to it during your commute.
entries.action: To remember better: - Listen and repeat: Say key points aloud after hearing them. - Mix modalities: Write down spoken info or speak aloud written notes. - Review audio: Record important notes and listen back later. Example: After a meeting, record a summary of key points and listen to it during your commute.
entries.check_in: Check in when you use a mix of listening and writing to strengthen recall.
keywords: Boost Recall with the Modality Effect

entries.title: Remember Something: - Make It Weird: Add Something Bizarre or Unusual to the Idea
entries.description: To remember something: - Make it weird: Add something bizarre or unusual to the idea or fact. - Visualize it vividly: Picture the bizarre element as vividly as possible. - Tell a story: Embed the information in a strange, memorable scenario. Example: To remember someone’s name (e.g., Daisy), imagine them wearing a giant daisy hat.
entries.action: To remember something: - Make it weird: Add something bizarre or unusual to the idea or fact. - Visualize it vividly: Picture the bizarre element as vividly as possible. - Tell a story: Embed the information in a strange, memorable scenario. Example: To remember someone’s name (e.g., Daisy), imagine them wearing a giant daisy hat.
entries.check_in: Check in when you use bizarre imagery to enhance your memory of something.

entries.title: Replace grand claims with a grounded statement and one next action.
entries.description: Turn a vague positive statement into words you can presently stand behind, connect it to one action under your control, and revise the statement when it becomes false, empty, or unhelpful.
entries.action: Write the positive statement you are tempted to use, underline the part that feels exaggerated or outside your control, replace it with language you can currently stand behind, attach one concrete action that would be consistent with the statement, and review the wording after you act.
entries.check_in: Can I honestly endorse this statement now, what action does it point to, and should I keep, narrow, or replace the wording after seeing what I actually did?
keywords: Say It Like You Mean It

entries.title: Retain the Message: - Summarize: Write or Say the Main Idea in Your Own
entries.description: To retain the message: - Summarize: Write or say the main idea in your own words. - Look for patterns: Identify recurring themes or key points. - Practice context recall: Remember when and why something was said, not just how. Example: After a meeting, jot down the core decisions and action points instead of trying to recall word-for-word what was said.

entries.check_in: Check in when you remember the essence of a conversation or reading.

entries.title: Rethink Default Quantities
entries.description: When consuming (e.g., food, resources): - Ask yourself: "Do I really need this much, or am I just following the default?" - Adjust portions: Take only what’s appropriate for your needs, not the suggested amount. - Set your own limits: Avoid letting external standards dictate your consumption. Example: Served a large plate of food? Eat until you’re satisfied, not until the plate is empty.

Example: Served a large plate of food? Eat until you’re satisfied, not until the plate is empty.
entries.check_in: Check in when you adjust consumption based on your actual needs.

entries.title: Review a Decision Using What Was Known at the Time
entries.description: Reconstruct what information was actually available when a decision was made, compare it with the options and constraints considered then, and turn the review into one process improvement for a similar future decision.
entries.action: Write the decision and its date, list the information and constraints that were available then, separate later discoveries into a different section, note which realistic alternatives were considered or missed, identify one process weakness or strength, and define one change to use for a similar future decision.
entries.check_in: What was genuinely knowable at the decision point, what did I learn only afterward, and what should change in the process next time?

entries.title: Review a High-Commitment Continue-or-Stop Decision
entries.description: For a commitment with multiple stakeholders, dependencies, or meaningful switching costs, compare future paths explicitly and document which current facts justify the next step.
entries.action: Define the feasible options. For each option record future cost, expected benefit, dependency or obligation, switching cost, reversibility, and important uncertainty. Ask what you would choose if the unrecoverable past investment were already accepted as history, then reconcile that answer with real current constraints.
entries.check_in: Which current facts justify continuing or stopping, which past costs are irrelevant to the next choice, and what uncertainty still matters?

entries.title: Review Open Tasks and Leave With a Clear Next Action
entries.description: Scan open work, remove or park stale items, clarify the next action for active commitments, and choose what deserves attention now without turning the review itself into a large planning project.
entries.action: Scan the open list, close or park items that are no longer active, rewrite vague active work as a concrete next action, identify blocked items and their dependency, choose the small set that deserves attention now, and stop the review before it turns into doing the tasks themselves.
entries.check_in: What became clearer, what was removed or parked, which item is blocked, and what is the next action I can actually take?

entries.title: Run a Detail Check Before You Ship
entries.description: Inspect a concrete artifact against a small checklist, run a second pass from a different angle, log anomalies, and improve the checklist from real misses rather than training vague hypervigilance.
entries.action: Choose an artifact or environment where errors matter, write a short checklist from known failure modes, inspect once for completeness and once from a different perspective such as data consistency or user flow, record anomalies, fix them, and update the checklist when a new recurring miss appears.
entries.check_in: What defect or ambiguity did the check find, which checklist item caught it, and what recurring miss should change the next review?

entries.title: Run a Missing-Evidence Check Before a Decision
entries.description: When a vivid or recent example is dominating a decision, separate what is easy to recall from what is representative, then look for one missing denominator, counterexample, or relevant source.
entries.action: Write the example or story currently driving the decision. Ask whether it is representative or simply vivid, recent, or personal. Look for one counterexample and, when the decision warrants it, one relevant denominator, base rate, or source. Update the decision only as far as the new information supports.
entries.check_in: What information was easy to recall, what was missing, and did the additional evidence change the decision or only the level of uncertainty?

entries.title: Run a Short, Concrete Information Interview
entries.description: Ask permission, focus on one recent event, follow the sequence step by step and separate remembered facts, estimates and interpretation.
entries.action: Explain why you are asking and get permission. Ask the person to walk through the most recent relevant example. Use one question at a time about sequence, context, tools, decisions and uncertainty. Summarize what you heard and invite correction.
entries.check_in: What concrete sequence did I learn, what remains an estimate or interpretation, and what did the person correct?

entries.title: Run a Six-Perspective Thinking Pass
entries.description: Separate facts, reactions, risks, opportunities, alternatives, and process into distinct passes so a discussion can expose what is missing before choosing a next step.
entries.action: Write one question. Make six short passes: facts and unknowns; reactions and preferences; risks and failure modes; benefits and opportunities; alternatives and experiments; then process and next step. Keep observations in their own pass so facts are not silently mixed with preferences or forecasts.
entries.check_in: Which perspective added information the first discussion was missing, and what decision, question, or test follows from it?
keywords: Try de Bono’s Six Thinking Hats

entries.title: Run a Weekly Review That Produces One Clear Change
entries.description: Use a recurring weekly checkpoint to inspect active goals, completed and missed work, constraints, and changing priorities, then turn the review into a small set of concrete scheduling or scope decisions.
entries.action: Review the active goals and commitments, note what moved and what did not, identify the main constraint or changed assumption, decide what should continue, stop, shrink, delegate, or move, and schedule the first concrete action created by the review.
entries.check_in: What moved this week, what blocked or changed, what am I changing for the next week, and where is the first action scheduled?

entries.title: Run One Disconfirming Check Before a Consequential Commitment
entries.description: Before an ordinary consequential commitment, state the assumption you currently favor, name one observable condition that would weaken it, check that condition directly, and update, narrow or escalate the decision when the result matters.
entries.action: Write the assumption driving the decision, state one observation that would materially weaken it, identify where that information can be checked, inspect it before the commitment becomes difficult to reverse, and then keep, narrow, change or escalate the plan according to what you found.
entries.check_in: What assumption was I favoring, what would have weakened it, did I check that condition, and how did the result change the commitment?

entries.title: Screen Break Checkpoint
entries.description: Use a simple checkpoint during screen-heavy work: look away, change posture, and decide whether the next block still deserves your attention.
entries.action: At a natural breakpoint in a long screen session, look away from the display, relax your posture, and name the next task before returning.
entries.check_in: Did the pause make the next action clearer, or did it reveal that you should stop, switch, or rest?

entries.title: See Beyond Personality
entries.description: When analyzing behavior: - Ask for others: "What situations might have influenced their actions?" - Ask for yourself: "Am I underestimating my own tendencies in this scenario?" - Broaden the lens: Balance personality traits with situational influences for everyone. Example: If someone is late, consider traffic or unexpected delays, not just lack of punctuality.
entries.action: When analyzing behavior: - Ask for others: "What situations might have influenced their actions?" - Ask for yourself: "Am I underestimating my own tendencies in this scenario?" - Broaden the lens: Balance personality traits with situational influences for everyone. Example: If someone is late, consider traffic or unexpected delays, not just lack of punctuality.
entries.check_in: Check in when you evaluate behavior with both situational and personality factors in mind.

entries.title: See Beyond the Group Glow
entries.description: When evaluating a group: - Pause and observe: "Am I judging individuals or the group as a whole?" - Focus on specifics: Look at individual contributions or qualities instead of the overall impression. - Compare individually: Evaluate members one by one to get a clearer picture. Example: Judging team performance? Break it down into individual efforts, not just the group’s vibe.

Example: Judging team performance? Break it down into individual efforts, not just the group’s vibe.
entries.check_in: Check in when you assess individuals within a group independently.

entries.title: See the Individual in the Group
entries.description: When judging groups: - Challenge assumptions: Ask, "Does this apply to all members, or just one person?" - Seek evidence: Look for facts about the group, not just individual actions. - Avoid overgeneralizing: Treat group decisions as collective, not necessarily representative of everyone. Example: If one team member misses a deadline, don’t assume the entire team is unreliable.

Example: If one team member misses a deadline, don’t assume the entire team is unreliable.
entries.check_in: Check in when you evaluate groups without letting one person’s actions define the whole.
keywords: See the Individual in the Group

entries.title: See the Individual, Not the Group
entries.description: When thinking about other groups: - Pause assumptions: Ask yourself, "Am I generalizing based on the group?" - Get personal: Interact with individuals from the group to learn about their unique experiences. - Stay curious: Challenge stereotypes by seeking real, diverse examples. Example: If you think "All people from X group act this way," question that thought and find real-world exceptions.

Example: If you think "All people from X group act this way," question that thought and find real-world exceptions.
entries.check_in: Check in when you recognize individuality over group stereotypes.

entries.title: Separate Controllable Actions From Dependencies and Outcomes
entries.description: For a concern or desired outcome, separate actions you can directly perform from dependencies you can influence or only observe, choose one concrete next action, and define how waiting items will be revisited instead of repeatedly planning the outcome itself.
entries.action: Write the concern or desired outcome, list the actions you can directly perform, list dependencies or responses owned by others, identify outcomes you can only observe, choose one next action under your control, and give waiting items a review trigger rather than repeatedly treating them as current work.
entries.check_in: What action can I perform directly, what depends on someone or something else, what outcome can I only observe, and when will I revisit the waiting part?

entries.title: Separate Observation from Human-Like Interpretation
entries.description: Describe what a non-human animal, plant, machine or model did before assigning a human motive. Add a system-specific alternative and state what remains uncertain.
entries.action: Choose one behavior or output. Record only what you could point to or reproduce. Write the human-like interpretation you first considered, then add a system-specific alternative and one low-risk way to check between them. Keep uncertainty visible when you cannot check.
entries.check_in: What did I directly observe, what interpretation did I add, and what alternative or check changed my next action?

entries.title: Separate Observed Facts From Assumed Intent
entries.description: When an ordinary ambiguous event feels intentional, separate the observable facts from your interpretation, list plausible alternatives, check relevant information, and use a neutral clarification before treating intent as established.
entries.action: Write the observable event without motive language, mark the inferred intent as an interpretation, list other explanations that fit the known facts, check the information that is reasonably available, and ask a neutral clarifying question when another person can resolve the ambiguity.
entries.check_in: What did I directly observe, what intent did I infer, what else could explain it, and what information would actually distinguish those explanations?

entries.title: Separate Outcomes From Actions You Can Control
entries.description: Draw two circles; one for factors you can control and another for those you cannot. Set clear, achievable goals based on what’s within your control.
entries.action: Write down one concern, separate the outcome from the actions you can take, convert anything you can influence into one concrete behavior, and choose the next useful action without pretending you control the final result.
entries.check_in: What part of this situation was actually mine to act on, what remained outside my control, and did the sorting help me choose a clearer next step?
keywords: Focus on What You Can Do

entries.title: Separate Review Sessions Instead of Cramming
entries.description: For verbal material you need to recall later, divide repeated study across separate sessions instead of concentrating the same planned review into one sitting. Choose the gap in relation to the intended retention period, then check recall and adjust rather than following one universal schedule.
entries.action: Choose one set of verbal material and decide how long you need to retain it. Split the planned repetitions across at least two sessions separated by time. Use a longer gap when the required retention period is longer, then check final recall and adjust the next schedule instead of treating one interval as universally optimal.
entries.check_in: Did I separate the study episodes rather than cram them together, and did the chosen gap fit the period over which I needed to remember the material?
keywords: Use the Lag Effect for Learning

entries.title: Separate Traits from Perception
entries.description: When forming an impression: - Ask yourself: "Am I judging based on one good trait or the full picture?" - Challenge assumptions: Notice if a positive quality is influencing unrelated judgments. - Seek diverse feedback: Gather opinions from others to balance your perception. Example: A charismatic colleague may not always be the best leader—focus on skills, not charm.
entries.action: When forming an impression: - Ask yourself: "Am I judging based on one good trait or the full picture?" - Challenge assumptions: Notice if a positive quality is influencing unrelated judgments. - Seek diverse feedback: Gather opinions from others to balance your perception. Example: A charismatic colleague may not always be the best leader—focus on skills, not charm.
entries.check_in: Check in when you evaluate someone based on multiple traits, not just one standout quality.

entries.title: Set Positive Expectations
entries.description: To harness the Pygmalion Effect: - Encourage: Set realistic but optimistic expectations for others. - Support: Provide feedback and resources to help them succeed. - Monitor: Ensure your expectations align with their actual strengths and goals. Example: If mentoring someone, focus on their potential and emphasize progress over perfection.

Example: If mentoring someone, focus on their potential and emphasize progress over perfection.
entries.check_in: Check in when you set positive expectations and see improvements in performance.

entries.title: Shared-Value Option Map
entries.description: Map what each side values, where constraints differ, and which exchanges could create value without pretending every conflict has a win-win solution.
entries.action: List what each side wants, what each side can trade at relatively low cost, and two or three options that combine those differences. Then test the options with the other side.
entries.check_in: Did the conversation uncover a real trade, or are the interests still incompatible enough that a clear boundary or no-deal option is better?

entries.title: Short Resilience Reminder
entries.description: Create a short phrase that acknowledges difficulty without pretending it is easy, then points back to one action you can still control.
entries.action: Write one sentence in the form: This is difficult, and the next thing I can control is ___. Keep it specific to the current situation.
entries.check_in: Did the phrase lead to a concrete action, or did it become empty motivation that you repeated without changing anything?
keywords: Torch of Life (Keep the Flame Going)

entries.title: Specific Gratitude Note
entries.description: Write one to three specific things you appreciated and why they mattered. Keep the practice optional and factual; gratitude is not a requirement to feel positive or a substitute for care.
entries.action: Choose one to three concrete moments, people, resources or actions from the day. Write what happened and one sentence about why it mattered to you. Skip the practice when it feels forced or unhelpful.
entries.check_in: Did the note help you notice something specific, or did it feel mechanical, invalidating, or like another obligation? Keep, change, or drop it accordingly.

entries.title: Spend Each Week Focused on a Single Theme
entries.description: Spend each week focused on a single theme. Immerse yourself in everything related to that topic through reading, watching, and activities.
entries.action: Choose one narrow learning theme for the week, define one visible result for Friday, and complete at least one small practice rep on each day you work on it.
entries.check_in: Did I complete one practice rep? What was the main friction, and what should I change for the next rep?

entries.title: Spot and Challenge Hidden Biases
entries.description: When interacting or making decisions: - Pause and reflect: "Am I acting on assumptions based on someone’s background or appearance?" - Seek diverse input: Surround yourself with perspectives different from your own. - Use structured decision-making: Avoid snap judgments by following a clear process. Example: Hiring? Focus on qualifications and skills, not personal characteristics.
entries.action: When interacting or making decisions: - Pause and reflect: "Am I acting on assumptions based on someone’s background or appearance?" - Seek diverse input: Surround yourself with perspectives different from your own. - Use structured decision-making: Avoid snap judgments by following a clear process. Example: Hiring? Focus on qualifications and skills, not personal characteristics.
entries.check_in: Check in when you notice and challenge an unconscious bias.

entries.title: Spot Choice-Supportive Bias
entries.description: After making a decision: - Be honest: Reflect on whether your choice truly delivered the results you hoped for. - Compare alternatives: Consider how other options might have played out. - Learn for next time: Focus on improving future decisions rather than justifying past ones. Example: If you bought a gadget and it didn’t meet expectations, admit it instead of defending the purchase.

Example: If you bought a gadget and it didn’t meet expectations, admit it instead of defending the purchase.
entries.check_in: Check in when you objectively evaluate a decision rather than justifying it.

entries.title: Spot Euphoric Recall
entries.description: When reflecting on past events: - List the facts: Write down both positive and negative aspects of the memory. - Get perspective: Talk to others who shared the experience to balance your view. - Be realistic: Remind yourself that every memory has highs and lows. Example: If you recall an old job fondly, note the challenges you faced there to keep things balanced.
entries.action: When reflecting on past events: - List the facts: Write down both positive and negative aspects of the memory. - Get perspective: Talk to others who shared the experience to balance your view. - Be realistic: Remind yourself that every memory has highs and lows. Example: If you recall an old job fondly, note the challenges you faced there to keep things balanced.
entries.check_in: Check in when you identify a memory that feels overly positive and balance it with the full picture.

entries.title: Spot Illusory Correlations
entries.description: To avoid false connections: - Look for patterns: Ask yourself, “Is this really connected, or just a coincidence?” - Seek evidence: Check if there’s actual data supporting the relationship. - Stay objective: Write down facts separately and then compare. Example: If you think eating bananas always improves your mood, track it for a week to see if the pattern holds.

entries.check_in: Check in when you catch yourself assuming a connection without evidence.

entries.title: Start a Morning Stretch Routine
entries.description: Begin each day with a 10-minute stretch routine, increasing to 20 minutes over time.
entries.action: Use a short, gentle flexibility routine as a morning movement cue if that timing suits you. Move slowly only as far as is comfortable, start with a few simple movements, and build up gradually rather than forcing a fixed 10-to-20-minute progression.
entries.check_in: Did the movements feel comfortable and controlled? Did I stop or modify anything that caused pain or made me feel unwell, and is this routine still appropriate for me?

entries.title: Stay Positive: - Recall Wins: Write Down 3 Good Things That Happened Each Day
entries.description: To stay positive: - Recall wins: Write down 3 good things that happened each day. - Reframe negatives: Think about what you learned from a tough situation. - Celebrate progress: Look back on how far you’ve come. Example: At the end of the week, write a short note about your best moments to revisit later.
entries.action: To stay positive: - Recall wins: Write down 3 good things that happened each day. - Reframe negatives: Think about what you learned from a tough situation. - Celebrate progress: Look back on how far you’ve come. Example: At the end of the week, write a short note about your best moments to revisit later.
entries.check_in: Check in when you focus on positive moments and lessons from the past.

entries.title: Stay Sharp: - Double-Check: Look up Facts You Think You
entries.description: To stay sharp: - Double-check: Look up facts you think you "just know." - Ask questions: Challenge statements that feel familiar but unverified. - Don’t repeat unverified info: Sharing it reinforces the bias. Example: Before you repeat a fun “fact” you read online, spend 5 minutes confirming it.

Example: Before you repeat a fun “fact” you read online, spend 5 minutes confirming it.
entries.check_in: Check in when you challenge a statement that feels true just because it’s familiar.

entries.title: Stay Sharp: - Take Notes: Write Down Key Points from the Person Speaking Before
entries.description: To stay sharp: - Take notes: Write down key points from the person speaking before you. - Breathe and listen: Avoid rehearsing your own response while someone else is speaking. - Repeat mentally: After someone speaks, quickly repeat their main point in your head. Example: In a team meeting, note what the person before you says and reference it when it’s your turn.
entries.action: To stay sharp: - Take notes: Write down key points from the person speaking before you. - Breathe and listen: Avoid rehearsing your own response while someone else is speaking. - Repeat mentally: After someone speaks, quickly repeat their main point in your head. Example: In a team meeting, note what the person before you says and reference it when it’s your turn.
entries.check_in: Check in when you stay present during group conversations and recall the last speaker's points.
keywords: Focus During Your Turn in Groups

entries.title: Stress-Test a Belief With Strong Counter-Information
entries.description: Write the specific claim you currently accept, note the strongest support you have, seek credible information that could challenge it, compare relevance and independence, then keep, narrow or revise the claim without giving weak counterclaims equal weight.
entries.action: Write the claim precisely, record what currently supports it, identify what kind of information would materially challenge it, seek the strongest relevant counter-information you can verify, compare source directness, relevance and independence, and record whether the claim stays, narrows or changes.
entries.check_in: What is the exact claim, what currently supports it, what strong counter-information did I find, and did I keep, narrow or revise the claim for a stated reason?

entries.title: Structure Dense Writing for Fast Navigation
entries.description: Turn a dense draft into a navigable document by giving each section one job and choosing headings, tables, diagrams, or images according to the information the reader needs to inspect.
entries.action: Name the reader's main task, read the current headings without the body, reorganize sections around that path, replace repeated comparisons with a table when rows share the same attributes, use a diagram for relationships or sequence, and keep images only when they show information that prose would make harder to inspect.
entries.check_in: Can a reader scan the headings and understand the path, and does every visual element answer a question that the surrounding text does not answer as clearly?

entries.title: Summarize with AI, Then Reconcile Against the Source
entries.description: For a long document you are allowed to process, ask AI for a structured summary tied to the source, then verify the claims that will affect a decision, message, or deliverable. The summary is navigation; the source remains the authority.
entries.action: Provide only material you are permitted to share. Ask for a summary with sections, explicit uncertainties, and source locations when available. Mark the claims that affect your decision, then open the source and verify those claims directly before reusing them.
entries.check_in: Can I point from every important statement in my final output back to the original source rather than to the AI summary?

entries.title: Take a Short Walk When Stress Builds
entries.description: Whenever stress hits, take a quick 10-minute walk—whether it’s outside, around a park, or just circling your office.
entries.action: When stress is building, consider a short, comfortable walk if walking is safe and practical for you. Treat ten minutes as a convenient boundary, not a medically proven dose. If a greener route is just as easy and safe, prefer it as a reasonable experiment rather than making a special trip. Then notice whether you feel any different before returning to the next task.
entries.check_in: Did I take the walk? Was the route ordinary or relatively green? How did my stress or tension feel before and after, and did I return more able to continue the next task?

entries.title: Talk About a Fear With Someone You Trust
entries.description: Share your fears with a trusted friend, family member, or therapist.
entries.action: Choose someone you trust and tell them, in your own words, what you are worried or afraid about. You can also say what kind of support you want, such as listening, practical help, or simply company. Keep the conversation within boundaries that feel appropriate for both of you.
entries.check_in: Who did I talk to, what did I want from the conversation, did I feel heard or supported, and is there any next step I need?

entries.title: Taste and Adjust One Variable at a Time
entries.description: For food that is safe to taste, sample at useful stages, identify the specific imbalance you notice, make one small adjustment, and taste again before changing something else.
entries.action: Choose a useful tasting point, make sure the food is safe and cool enough to sample, name the issue you notice such as blandness, excess salt, acidity, texture, or thickness, choose one small adjustment appropriate to the dish, mix or cook as needed, then taste again before making another change.
entries.check_in: What did I notice before the adjustment, what single change did I make, and what is different after the next safe taste?

entries.title: Test a New Work Tool on a Low-Risk Task
entries.description: Pick one recurring work problem, try one tool on a noncritical task, compare the old and new workflow, then keep, adjust, or drop it based on what you observe.
entries.action: Choose one recurring low-risk work task, note how you handle it now, try one new tool on a test or noncritical case, compare the result and friction, and decide whether to repeat, adjust, or stop.
entries.check_in: What task did I test, what changed in the workflow, what friction appeared, and is the next step to keep, adjust, or drop the tool?

entries.title: Test the Truth
entries.description: When someone shares information: - Ask for clarity: "Where did you hear this?" or "What’s the source?" - Cross-check: Verify their claims with other evidence. - Stay neutral: Don’t assume truth or falsehood—investigate first. Example: A colleague makes a bold claim in a meeting. Instead of accepting it outright, request data or examples.
entries.action: When someone shares information: - Ask for clarity: "Where did you hear this?" or "What’s the source?" - Cross-check: Verify their claims with other evidence. - Stay neutral: Don’t assume truth or falsehood—investigate first. Example: A colleague makes a bold claim in a meeting. Instead of accepting it outright, request data or examples.
entries.check_in: Check in when you verify information instead of assuming its truth.

entries.title: Think Beyond Your Current Self
entries.description: When making future plans: - Pause: Ask, "Will future me feel the same way?" - Imagine different scenarios: Consider how changes in mood, priorities, or environment might affect your choices. - Build flexibility: Leave room to adapt as your preferences evolve. Example: Booking a gym membership? Think about whether your motivation will match your current enthusiasm in a month.

Example: Booking a gym membership? Think about whether your motivation will match your current enthusiasm in a month.
entries.check_in: Check in when you adjust a plan to account for changing future preferences.

entries.title: Think Off the Bandwagon
entries.description: When considering a popular opinion: - Pause: Ask yourself, "Do I agree because it’s popular or because it’s right?" - Analyze: Break down the reasoning behind the opinion. Does it align with your values or evidence? - Decide independently: Make choices based on your evaluation, not peer pressure. Example: A team might agree on a subpar idea because everyone else does. Challenge it with better logic.

Does it align with your values or evidence? - Decide independently: Make choices based on your evaluation, not peer pressure. Example: A team might agree on a subpar idea because everyone else does. entries.title: Trace Repeated Claims Back to Their Underlying Sources
entries.description: When several pages or reports repeat the same claim, follow their links and citations back to the underlying material, record shared documents, datasets or organizations, and distinguish independent origins from repeated summaries.
entries.action: Write the claim, list the pages or reports repeating it, follow their citations or links toward the origin, note shared documents, datasets, organizations or copied wording, and classify the set as independent origins, shared origin, mixed, or unclear.
entries.check_in: Which items looked separate, what underlying origin did each one use, where did they overlap, and how many genuinely distinct origins remain?

entries.title: Translate a Problem into a Nature-Inspired Design Principle
entries.description: Describe the function a solution must perform, inspect a biological example, extract a transferable principle and test one safe application without copying the organism literally.
entries.action: State what the solution must do without naming the current solution. Choose a biological example from a reliable description. Separate the observed structure or process from the metaphor. Write one transferable principle, generate several applications and test the smallest reversible option within safety and operational constraints.
entries.check_in: What function did I study, what principle did I extract, and what did the small test reveal about its usefulness or limit?

entries.title: Try a Short Breath Meditation
entries.description: Sit somewhere safe, let your breathing stay natural, notice when attention wanders, and bring it back. If starting is the hard part, you can attach the practice to a stable daily routine. The cue is an implementation option, not a proven adherence hack, and five minutes is still a convenient container rather than a therapeutic dose.
entries.action: Sit somewhere comfortable and safe. Let breathing stay natural. Notice the sensations of breathing; when attention drifts into plans, memories, sounds or commentary, notice that and return to the breath without grading yourself. Use five minutes only if it is a convenient starting container. If initiation is the problem, choose one recurring non-safety-critical cue — for example after closing the laptop for lunch or after finishing your evening hygiene — and let that cue mean 'try the short practice now.' After several attempts, keep the cue only if it reduces friction without making the practice annoying or compulsory.
entries.check_in: Did I notice attention wandering and return without turning it into a fight? If I used a routine cue, did it actually make starting easier? Was the practice useful, neutral or uncomfortable? Would another wellbeing practice fit me better today?

entries.title: Try Progressive Muscle Relaxation Gently
entries.description: Tightly squeeze each muscle group for five seconds, then relax it for thirty seconds, moving from your toes up to your head.
entries.action: Sit or lie somewhere comfortable and work through a few muscle groups one at a time. Gently tense each group for no more than about five seconds, then release it and notice the contrast. Do not strain, and skip or release any area that causes significant discomfort. If sleep is your target, use PMR as a repeatable wind-down experiment rather than a one-night sleep test.
entries.check_in: Did I practise without pain or straining? If I am using PMR for sleep, across several attempts did winding down or my subjective sleep feel meaningfully easier, unchanged, or worse?

entries.title: Try Quiet Wakeful Rest After Learning
entries.description: After learning declarative material you want to remember, try a short period of quiet, minimally stimulating wakeful rest before switching to another demanding task. Treat it as a personal memory experiment, not a general learning upgrade or a universal ten-minute rule.
entries.action: When you finish a focused memory-heavy learning episode, put aside the material and spend a brief period awake in a quiet, low-stimulation setting. Avoid immediately switching to another cognitively demanding task. Choose a duration that is practical for you, then return to normal activity. Do not use the pause as a substitute for self-testing, active review, or other learning methods.
entries.check_in: What did I learn, did I actually create a low-interference pause afterward, and when I checked later did recall seem better, unchanged, or worse than usual?

entries.title: Try Short High-Intensity Intervals Safely
entries.description: Perform a HIIT session with 20 seconds of intense exercise (like sprinting or jumping jacks) followed by 10 seconds of rest, repeated for 8 rounds.
entries.action: If vigorous exercise is appropriate for your current fitness and health, choose a simple movement you can perform safely. You can use it as one short interval session, or as brief exercise snacks separated across the day when a full workout is unlikely. Make the effort challenging but controlled. Treat 20/10, 3 × 1 minute, 4 × 1 minute and similar timers as formats to adapt, not scientifically optimized doses.
entries.check_in: Was the effort genuinely challenging but still controlled, could I repeat it without losing movement quality, and over several weeks is fitness or function trending in a useful direction rather than just my streak count?

entries.title: Turn a Good Intention into an If-Then Plan
entries.description: Turn a repeated low-stakes choice into a simple cue-and-action rule, add a fallback for common exceptions, and revise the rule when it creates friction or no longer fits the work.
entries.action: Choose one repeated situation, describe the cue in observable terms, choose a small action you can safely perform when the cue appears, add a fallback for a common exception, use the rule when the situation occurs, and revise or retire it when it stops fitting the work.
entries.check_in: Did the cue occur, did I follow the chosen action, what exception appeared, and should the rule stay, change, or be removed?

entries.title: Turn a Large Goal into the Next Verifiable Step
entries.description: Define the finish condition, expose dependencies, split the goal into observable deliverables, and choose the smallest next step that creates information or progress.
entries.action: Write what done looks like, list the major deliverables and external dependencies, split uncertain work until each next step has an observable output, choose the smallest useful step, complete it, and update the map from what you learned.
entries.check_in: What became complete or clearer, what dependency blocks the next step, and what is the smallest observable deliverable now?

entries.title: Turn a Screen-Free Meeting Into a Walking Meeting
entries.description: Use a walking meeting to replace part of a long sitting block when the conversation does not require a screen. Evidence supports the movement break, not a special meeting effect.
entries.action: When a meeting is mostly listening and talking, replace some of that sitting with an easy walk if the route, weather, privacy and meeting format make it safe. Keep screen-heavy or safety-critical conversations seated. Capture decisions before you finish.
entries.check_in: Did I replace a sitting block with walking without making the meeting worse? Was the route safe and the conversation easy enough to follow? Would I use this format again for this kind of meeting?

entries.title: Turn an AI Reflection into One Next Action
entries.description: Give an AI assistant a concrete goal, current constraints, and the decision you need to make; ask for options, assumptions, and failure modes; verify factual claims; then choose one reversible next action yourself.
entries.action: State one concrete goal or decision, provide the relevant constraints and what you already know, ask the AI for a small set of distinct options with assumptions and failure modes, challenge anything vague, verify factual claims that matter, choose one reversible next action yourself, and record what would cause you to change course.
entries.check_in: What became clearer, which AI claim still needs verification, what action did I choose, and what new information would make me revise the decision?
keywords: Chat with Coot.AI: Personal Growth Conversations

entries.title: Turn Meeting Notes into Actions, Then Reconcile Them
entries.description: After a meeting, use AI to convert permitted notes or a transcript into decisions, actions, owners, dates, and open questions. Then reconcile the structured output against the original record before it becomes the team's memory.
entries.action: Use only notes or transcripts you are allowed to process. Ask for five buckets: decisions, actions, owners, dates, and unresolved questions. Compare each populated field with the source, remove inferred commitments, and publish the checked version quickly while context is fresh.
entries.check_in: Does every named owner and commitment come from the meeting, or did the model quietly turn a suggestion into an assignment?

entries.title: Turn One Routine Exchange into a Genuine Micro-Conversation
entries.description: When the situation is relaxed and the other person seems willing, make one routine exchange slightly more human: eye contact, a real greeting, or a brief conversation. Treat it as a small social opportunity, not a cure for loneliness.
entries.action: Pick an ordinary low-pressure interaction that already needs to happen: buying coffee, greeting a neighbor, talking to a receptionist, or another brief exchange. If the context is appropriate, make eye contact, greet the person, and add one natural sentence or question. Keep it short and responsive to the other person's cues. If they are busy, uncomfortable, or not interested, let the interaction stay efficient.
entries.check_in: Did the interaction feel more connected without becoming intrusive, and did the other person seem willing to engage?

entries.title: Turn Real Examples into a Draft SOP with AI
entries.description: When a recurring task lives mostly in someone's head, give AI a few sanitized examples and ask for a draft procedure with inputs, steps, decisions, outputs, and exceptions. Validate the draft with the person who does the work and test it on a fresh case before treating it as process documentation.
entries.action: Choose several representative examples and remove information you should not share. Ask AI to separate inputs, steps, decisions, outputs, exceptions, and unresolved questions. Review the draft with the actual operator, then run one new case using only the SOP and revise where the procedure breaks.
entries.check_in: Could another competent person complete a fresh case from the checked SOP without relying on the hidden knowledge that created the examples?

entries.title: Uncover Hidden Insights
entries.description: In group discussions: - Encourage: Ask each member to share unique perspectives or information. - Facilitate: Guide the conversation to ensure unshared insights are discussed. - Balance: Avoid spending too much time on what everyone already knows. Example: Start meetings by asking, "What does everyone know that hasn’t been shared yet?"
entries.action: In group discussions: - Encourage: Ask each member to share unique perspectives or information. - Facilitate: Guide the conversation to ensure unshared insights are discussed. - Balance: Avoid spending too much time on what everyone already knows. Example: Start meetings by asking, "What does everyone know that hasn’t been shared yet?"
entries.check_in: Check in when you prioritize new or unique insights during a discussion.

entries.title: Understand Context in Behavior
entries.description: When judging behavior: - For others: Ask, "What situations might have influenced their actions?" - For yourself: Reflect, "How much of this is about my choices versus circumstances?" - Balance the view: Consider both personality and context for all parties. Example: A colleague misses a deadline—consider if external factors, not just laziness, played a role.

Example: A colleague misses a deadline—consider if external factors, not just laziness, played a role.
entries.check_in: Check in when you evaluate behavior by considering both personality and situational factors.

entries.title: Understand Motivations
entries.description: When evaluating motivation: - For others: Ask, "Could their actions come from genuine interest, not just external rewards?" - For yourself: Reflect, "Are my actions really driven by passion, or am I influenced by external factors?" - Compare honestly: Treat others’ motivations as complex as your own. Example: A teammate working late might care about the project, not just a bonus.
